quiz.explain: Calculated fields work on sums, never counts; use Average of principal in Values, or a column of 1s (→ section 1, A calculated field; P7).

quiz.q: Which chart for disbursements by month over 34 months?
options: A pie, one slice per month
A line, with a 3-month moving average for the trend
A 3D column chart
A stacked bar sorted by amount
quiz.explain: Time on the x-axis is a line's job; the moving average is the trend, the monthly line the noise (→ section 1, Which chart for which question; section 6).

quiz.q: Which chart rules are not matters of taste?
options: Bars and columns start at zero
No 3D
The title states the finding
Use a pie whenever you show shares
Give every bar its own colour
quiz.explain: A pie hides small slices, and one colour plus one highlight keeps the eye on the point (→ section 1, Chart trap: the pie with many slices; Building an honest chart).

quiz.q: Two branches have 150 and 160 bn outstanding. The column chart's axis starts at 140 bn. How many times taller does the 160 bar LOOK than the 150 bar?
quiz.code: bar heights drawn: 160 − 140 and 150 − 140
quiz.explain: 20 vs 10 units: the eye reads 'twice as big' for a 7 % difference — bars start at zero (→ section 1, Chart trap: the truncated axis; section 2, step 9).

quiz.q: Power Query refreshed this morning with new loans, but the pivot still shows last week's totals. Why?
options: Pivots cannot read queries
The pivot reads its own cache; it updates only on Refresh (or Refresh All)
The slicer is hiding the new rows
Pivots ignore rows added after creation
quiz.explain: Build on a Table or query output and refresh the pivot after the data (→ section 1, Refresh, the pivot cache and formats that survive it; P10).

quiz.q: A pivot is filtered to the Top 5 branches. You divide its Grand Total by itself to get 'share of the book'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing
A filtered pivot's Grand Total is the total of the shown rows only, so the share comes out 100 %; divide by the Table's SUM instead
Top-N filters do not change totals
GETPIVOTDATA is required
quiz.explain: The denominator must come from the unfiltered book (→ P4).

quiz.q: On 1 October the Disbursements MTD tile shows 21 loans, 0.85 bn. What belongs on the tile?
options: Only those numbers
Those numbers labelled as one day, with the last full month (September) beside them
Replace them with September's numbers silently
Hide the tile until the month ends
quiz.explain: A partial period must be marked, never compared with full months without a note (→ section 6, Company corner).

w04d5.t: Week 4 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: cleaned dataset + one-page report

quiz.q: After Refresh All, customers_clean still contains ids above 6 000. What went wrong?
options: The duplicate key was wrong
No Sort on registered_at before Remove Duplicates, so the later copy was kept instead of the original
Remove Duplicates was run twice
The ids were typed as text
quiz.explain: Remove Duplicates keeps the first row it meets; sort so the row you want to keep comes first (→ A1, model answer; If you are stuck).

quiz.q: Three customers' monthly_income (in millions). One blank was typed as 0 during cleaning. What does AVERAGE now return?
quiz.code:
monthly_income: 10 | 20 | 0   (the 0 was a blank)

=AVERAGE(customers_clean[monthly_income])
quiz.explain: With the blank kept as null, AVERAGE skips it and returns 15; a zero income is a statement, a blank is a gap (→ A1, checks).

quiz.q: 24 payments are dated after 2026-10-01. What does payments_clean do with them?
options: Deletes them
Keeps them, flags them with is_forward_dated, and excludes them from as-of sums
Changes their date to 2026-10-01
Moves them to a separate file
quiz.explain: They are real payments recorded with a future date: nothing destroyed, flagged, filtered where an as-of matters (→ A2).

quiz.q: The reviewer duplicates the last line of payments_dirty.csv and presses Refresh All. What must payments_clean show?
options: One row more than before
The same row count as before — the new line is one more copy of a known payment
An error
Zero rows
quiz.explain: The cleaning is a property of the query, not of the file; a count that changes means something was pasted (→ What the reviewer runs).

quiz.q: Which choices keep the one-pager refreshable?
options: Data arrives through Power Query or a Table
Pivots are built on the Table or query output
Tiles read the pivots with GETPIVOTDATA or the Table with SUMIFS
Number formats are set in Value Field Settings
Pivots built on a fixed range A1:M7829
Tiles pasted as values before sending
quiz.explain: A fixed range never grows and a pasted value never updates (→ Part C, question 8; Common mistakes).

quiz.q: XLOOKUP returns #N/A for a product that is clearly in the Lookup table. What is the likely cause?
quiz.code:
A2 shows: Micro loan
=LEN(A2)  → 11
options: XLOOKUP needs FALSE as the last argument
A trailing space in the key — 'Micro loan' has 10 characters; TRIM it
The Lookup table is not sorted
The product is in a hidden row
quiz.explain: #N/A means nothing matched: check spaces with LEN and numbers stored as text with ISNUMBER (→ Follow-ups a panel asks).

quiz.q: Finance says September's collection rate is 96 %; your tile says 94.1 %. What do you answer?
options: One of the two is a formula error
Different bases: cash basis (all money received in September ÷ due) vs instalment basis (paid on September's instalments ÷ due); both right, name the basis
Finance used dirty payments
Round both to 95 %
quiz.explain: Write the basis under the tile and the argument ends (→ Follow-ups a panel asks; Day 3, Company corner).

quiz.q: Which sentence belongs in findings.md?
options: Chart 1 shows outstanding by product.
PAR30 is 3.12 % and NPL90 2.55 %, so most at-risk money is already past 90 days: old debt, not a new wave.
I used a pivot table on tblLoans.
The page has six tiles.
quiz.explain: Each finding carries a number and a consequence the board can act on (→ Part B, findings note).

quiz.q: tblApplications[status] holds 'approved' (7 917 rows), 'approved_not_disbursed' (678), 'rejected' (3 588) and 'cancelled' (1 817). What does this formula return?
quiz.code: =COUNTIFS(tblApplications[status], "approved*")
quiz.explain: The * wildcard matches any ending, so it counts 'approved' and 'approved_not_disbursed': 7 917 + 678 = 8 595. With plain "approved" you get 7 917 and an approval rate of 56.6 % instead of 61.4 %. Wildcards work in COUNTIFS and SUMIFS criteria, not with = (→ Week 4 · Day 1, Wildcards in criteria).

quiz.q: The fourth argument is missing. What does Excel do?
quiz.code: =VLOOKUP(D2, Lookup!$A$2:$F$7, 3)
options: Exact match: it shows #N/A when the key is not found
Approximate match: on a list that is not sorted it can return a neighbour's value, with no error
It refuses to calculate and shows #VALUE!
It searches the list from the bottom
quiz.explain: Without FALSE, VLOOKUP assumes a sorted list and does an approximate match: a wrong rate, nothing red. Always write FALSE, or use XLOOKUP, which is exact by default (→ Week 4 · Day 2, VLOOKUP and its four traps).

quiz.q: The bucket table holds the upper edge of each band. Which bucket does dpd 31 get, and why?
quiz.code:
edge | bucket
0    | 0
30   | 1-30
60   | 31-60
90   | 61-90

=XLOOKUP(31, edge, bucket, , -1)
options: 31-60, which is right
1-30: with upper edges and match mode -1, a value just above an edge falls one band too low
#N/A, because 31 is not in the table
quiz.explain: Match mode -1 returns the next smaller edge, 30, so the label is 1-30 and no error warns you. Key the table on the lower edges (0, 1, 31, 61, 91) with -1, or on upper edges with mode 1 (→ Week 4 · Day 2, XLOOKUP for bands).

quiz.q: A lookup misses for some loans, and a SUM sits under this column. What does the IFERROR do to the total?
quiz.code: =IFERROR(XLOOKUP([@product], Lookup!$A$2:$A$7, Lookup!$C$2:$C$7), 0)
options: Nothing: it only hides the #N/A
It turns every miss into a zero, so the total looks complete and is short, and nobody sees the misses
It makes the SUM return #N/A
It adds the missing rows to the lookup table
quiz.explain: IFERROR(…, 0) is for an error you expect and understand. Around a lookup under a SUM it hides the misses inside the total. Count the misses first (COUNTIF of the errors, or a check cell) and let them show (→ Week 4 · Day 2, IFERROR).

quiz.q: A1 holds 6 507 526 953 (outstanding of loans with DPD over 30) and A2 holds 208 723 504 430 (all outstanding). C1 has this formula and the cell format Percentage with no decimals. What does C1 show? Type the number.
quiz.explain: A1/A2 is 0.0312, and the Percentage format multiplies by 100 again: 100 × 0.0312 = 3.12, shown as 312 %. Write =A1/A2 and let the format do the ×100: 3 % (3.12 % with two decimals) (→ Week 4 · Day 1, Number formats vs values).

quiz.q: Outstanding is in millions of soum. What does this formula return?
quiz.code:
row | A loan_id | B branch          | C status | D disbursed_at | E dpd | F outstanding
2   | 101       | Tashkent South    | active   | 2026-08-14     | 0     | 100
3   | 102       | Fergana Central   | active   | 2026-09-03     | 12    | 50
4   | 103       | Tashkent North    | default  | 2025-11-20     | 95    | 40
5   | 104       | Tashkent South    | active   | 2026-09-28     | 45    | 30
6   | 105       | Fergana Central   | closed   | 2026-10-01     | 0     | 0

=SUMIFS(F2:F6, B2:B6, "Tashkent*", E2:E6, ">0")
quiz.explain: Two conditions, both must hold: the branch starts with Tashkent (rows 2, 4 and 5) and dpd is above 0 (rows 3, 4 and 5). Rows 4 and 5 meet both: 40 + 30 = 70. Every pair of criteria is one more AND (→ Week 4 · Day 1, Several criteria; Wildcards in criteria).

quiz.q: A column of dates looks right, but COUNTIFS with a date criterion returns a count that is too low, and nothing turns red. What is the most likely cause?
options: Some dates are stored as text, and date criteria skip them
COUNTIFS is case-sensitive
The Table has a Total Row
The criteria range is shorter than the count range
quiz.explain: A date stored as text looks like a date and is skipped by every date criterion. Check with =ISNUMBER(D2), which must say TRUE, and convert with DATEVALUE or Power Query. Unequal ranges would give #VALUE! (→ Week 4 · Day 1, Dates in criteria; Day 3, Dates stored as text).

quiz.q: Column B holds 10, an empty cell, 20 and a typed 0. What does =AVERAGE(B2:B5) return?
quiz.explain: AVERAGE skips the empty cell but counts the typed 0: (10 + 20 + 0) / 3 = 10. Never fill blanks with 0 to tidy up: the average income of the customers would fall from 15 245 933 to 14 347 331 (→ Week 4 · Day 1, SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT).

quiz.q: Which Power Query command turns many value columns into rows (one word)?
quiz.explain: Unpivot turns wide columns into two columns, Attribute (the old header) and Value, one row per old cell. It is the opposite of a pivot (→ Week 4 · Day 3, Unpivot).

quiz.q: Which of these give a wrong pivot table?
options: The pivot is built on a fixed range, A1:K7829
Values uses Average of outstanding when the sentence asks for a share or a rate
The pivot sits on the instalments table and sums a loan-level column such as principal
The pivot is built on a Table or on the output of a query
Refresh All is pressed twice
quiz.explain: A fixed range never receives new rows. An average of rates weights a small loan like a large one: use a calculated field (a ratio of sums). Summing a loan column on instalment rows counts each principal once per instalment: know the grain. A Table or query as the source is the correct way, and a second Refresh All is harmless (→ Week 4 · Day 4, pivot traps).

quiz.q: In a pivot you add a calculated field avg_ticket = principal / loan_id. What does it compute?
options: The average principal per loan
The sum of principal divided by the sum of the loan ids: a meaningless number, with no error
The number of loans
#DIV/0!
quiz.explain: A calculated field sees sums only; there is no COUNT inside it. Use Average of principal in Values, or two sums and a formula (→ Week 4 · Day 4, A calculated field).

quiz.q: The monthly line chart ends with October 2026 and drops by about 95 %. What is the problem?
options: Nothing: October is a bad month
October holds one day of data (21 loans), plotted as a full month: leave it out or mark it as partial
The chart needs a dual axis
The axis should start at 15 bn
quiz.explain: The data stops on 1 October: 852 760 000 against 17 015 490 000 in September, a fake drop of 95 %. A partial period compared with full ones always looks like a crash (→ Week 4 · Day 4, Show Values As; Chart traps).

quiz.q: Which of these make a chart misleading?
options: A bar chart whose axis starts at 150 bn
A 3D pie chart
A dual axis with two unrelated measures, so the lines cross
A line chart of 34 monthly points
A chart title that states the finding
quiz.explain: A bar axis that does not start at zero makes a small gap look huge; a 3D pie makes the front slice look bigger; a dual axis makes two lines cross for no reason. A line over many months and a title with the finding are the right choices (→ Week 4 · Day 4, Chart traps; Building an honest chart).

quiz.q: What is wrong with this formula?
quiz.code: =FILTER(tblLoans, AND(tblLoans[dpd] > 30, tblLoans[status] = "active"))
options: Nothing, it returns the active loans over 30 days late
AND returns one TRUE or FALSE for the whole column; write (a)*(b) instead
FILTER cannot read a Table
The status must be written in capitals
quiz.explain: Inside FILTER and SUMPRODUCT, AND and OR do not work row by row. Write AND as (a)*(b) and OR as (a)+(b) (→ Week 4 · Day 2, FILTER; Day 1, AND, OR, NOT).

quiz.q: In Power Query you Merge loans (7 828 rows) with a table that holds two rows for some loan_id. The result has more than 7 828 rows. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The merge is a Left Outer; switch to Inner
The bottom table has more than one row per key, so the merge multiplies the top rows; Group By it to one row per key first
Power Query adds a total row
The loan_id column is typed as text
quiz.explain: It is the one-to-many trap of week 2, in Power Query. Count the rows after every merge, and reduce the bottom table to one row per key first (→ Week 4 · Day 3, Merge Queries).

quiz.q: B2 is empty (a blank credit score). What does this formula show?
quiz.code: =IF(B2 >= 600, "pass", "check")
options: pass
check
no score
#VALUE!
quiz.explain: An empty cell counts as 0 in a test, so the blank gets the same answer as a low score. Test for blank first: =IF(B2="", "no score", IF(B2>=600, "pass", "check")) (→ Week 4 · Day 1, IF).

quiz.q: Why does this query fail?
quiz.code:
SELECT product_id, COUNT(*)
FROM loans
WHERE COUNT(*) > 300
GROUP BY product_id;
options: When WHERE runs, no count exists yet; the condition on a count belongs in HAVING
COUNT(*) cannot be used with GROUP BY
There must be an ORDER BY
loans has no product_id
quiz.explain: The order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT. WHERE filters rows before any group exists; HAVING filters the groups after they are counted (→ Week 2 · Day 2, WHERE vs HAVING).

quiz.q: customers LEFT JOIN applications returns 14 587 rows. applications has 14 000 rows and every application belongs to a customer. How many customers never applied?
quiz.explain: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer: one row per application, plus one row with NULLs for each customer without an application. 14 587 − 14 000 = 587 (→ Week 2 · Day 1, LEFT JOIN; The anti-join).

quiz.q: Why is the second average lower than the first?
quiz.code:
SELECT AVG(monthly_income) FROM customers;                  -- 15 245 933
SELECT AVG(COALESCE(monthly_income, 0)) FROM customers;    -- 14 347 331
options: COALESCE invents 356 customers who earn nothing and averages them in
COALESCE rounds the income down
AVG skips the zeros
The second query reads fewer rows
quiz.explain: AVG skips NULL on its own, so the first query averages the 5 684 customers with an income. COALESCE(…, 0) turns the 356 empty incomes into zeros and counts them. Fill a NULL only when you can say what it means (→ Week 2 · Day 4, COALESCE).

quiz.q: SQLite and SQL Server alike. The loans table has 7 828 rows, and the terms add up to 92 193 months. What does this return?
quiz.code: SELECT SUM(term_months) / COUNT(*) FROM loans;
quiz.explain: 92 193 divided by 7 828 is 11.78, but a whole number divided by a whole number is a whole number: 11. Put 1.0 * in front, or use AVG(term_months), which gives 11.78 (→ Week 2 · Day 2, AVG; Day 3, Integer and decimal division).

quiz.q: What does the total column show on each row?
quiz.code:
SELECT product_id, loan_id, principal,
       SUM(principal) OVER (PARTITION BY product_id
                            ORDER BY disbursed_at, loan_id) AS total
FROM loans;
options: The sum of all principal in the table
A running total of principal within each product, in the order of disbursement
One total per product, with the rows collapsed
The row's own principal
quiz.explain: PARTITION BY restarts the sum for each product; ORDER BY inside OVER makes it a running total; the tiebreaker (, loan_id) keeps equal dates from jumping together. All rows stay (→ Week 3 · Day 1, ORDER BY inside OVER; The frame).

quiz.q: You de-duplicate payments with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY installment_id, paid_at, amount ORDER BY payment_id DESC) and keep rn = 1. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: the count is the same
The order decides which twin survives: DESC keeps the re-imported copies and deletes the originals, with the same count
ROW_NUMBER cannot be used with PARTITION BY
Every payment gets rn = 1
quiz.explain: The ORDER BY inside the window decides which row gets 1. The earliest payment_id is the original; ascending order keeps it (→ Week 3 · Day 2, Duplicates).

quiz.q: The Power BI tiles must all use one definition of DPD. What should they read?
options: Each tile has its own query with its own DPD formula
A view such as v_loan_status, or a nightly table built from it
A CSV that someone exported last month
A temporary table
quiz.explain: A view keeps one definition in one place: fix it once and every tile changes. A nightly table made from it is faster to read but frozen until the next load (→ Week 3 · Day 4, When a view, when a table).

quiz.q: Which line is the definition of PAR30?
options: The share of loans with DPD over 30, by count
Outstanding of loans with DPD over 30, divided by the total outstanding
Outstanding of loans with DPD over 90, divided by the total outstanding
The overdue amount divided by the principal lent
quiz.explain: PAR30 is portfolio at risk: the money still owed on loans more than 30 days late, as a share of all the money still owed. Option C is NPL90. Name the denominator next to the number (→ Week 1 · Day 3, Company corner; Week 3 · Day 5, S9).

quiz.q: strftime returns text. How many loans does each query find in September of any year?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans WHERE strftime('%m', disbursed_at) = 9;     -- A
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans WHERE strftime('%m', disbursed_at) = '09';  -- B
options: A finds 780, B finds 780
A finds 0, B finds 780
A finds 780, B finds 0
Both find 0
quiz.explain: The text '09' is not equal to the number 9, so A finds nothing and no error warns you. Compare with a two-digit text, or CAST the result to an integer (→ Week 2 · Day 3, strftime).

w05d1.t: Week 5 · Day 1 — Python from zero: the notebook is your lab

quiz.q: You change the function in cell 3, then re-run only cell 7, which calls it. Which version does cell 7 use?
options: Whichever cell is higher on the page
None — it raises NameError
The new one — Jupyter re-reads every cell above
The old one — the kernel remembers what was last run, not what is on the screen
quiz.explain: The kernel keeps variables in the order cells were run; Kernel → Restart & Run All is the only proof that a notebook works top to bottom (→ section 1, 'Where your code runs').

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
principal = "31150000"      # as read by csv.DictReader
print(principal * 2)
options: TypeError
quiz.explain: Every value from a CSV is text, and a string times 2 is the string repeated — convert with int() before any arithmetic (→ P1).

quiz.q: With label() from section 1, what does the last line print?
quiz.code:
def label(dpd):
    if dpd <= 0: return "0"
    elif dpd <= 30: return "1-30"
    elif dpd <= 60: return "31-60"
    elif dpd <= 90: return "61-90"
    else: return "90+"

print(label(30), label(91))
quiz.explain: dpd <= 30 is still 1-30, and 91 is past 90 — the right-closed buckets of week 2 (→ P6).

quiz.q: This loop gives approval rates a few points below week 4's 58.2 / 63.7 / 61.9 %. Why?
options: total.get(ch, 0) resets the count on every row
The rows were not converted with int()
The dicts are not sorted
== "approved" misses the approved_not_disbursed rows
quiz.explain: Status has two 'approved' spellings; startswith("approved") is week 4's "approved*" wildcard — == alone loses 678 approvals (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Approved / applications: app 2 915 / 5 006, branch 3 965 / 6 223, partner 1 715 / 2 771. What is the total approval rate, in %, one decimal?
quiz.explain: Sum the counts: 8 595 / 14 000 = 61.4 %. Averaging the three channel rates gives 61.3 % — never average rates for a total row (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Which statements about rows read with csv.DictReader are true?
options: Numeric columns are converted to int automatically
Every value is a string
A blank cell arrives as an empty string ""
Each row is a dict keyed by the header line
sum() skips blank credit scores by itself
quiz.explain: DictReader gives text keyed by the header; convert on use and test for "" first — 388 credit scores are blank (→ section 1, 'Reading a CSV').

quiz.q: A cell fails with a long traceback. What do you read first?
options: The first line
Nothing — re-run the cell until it works
The frames inside the library
The last line (the error type and message), then the arrow at your own code
quiz.explain: The newest call is at the bottom: the last line names the error, the arrow shows the line of your code (→ section 1, 'Errors').

quiz.q: Company corner: loan 1 (24-month annuity) is one year into its term. Its outstanding is…
options: the sum of the 12 remaining payments, interest included
more than 50 %, because the early payments are mostly interest
exactly 50 % of the principal
less than 50 %, because interest is paid off first
quiz.explain: Interest = balance × r is front-loaded, so the principal parts start small; outstanding = principal not yet due — 57 % for loan 1 (→ Company corner).

w05d2.t: Week 5 · Day 2 — pandas I: the DataFrame is a table you can talk to

quiz.q: The loan with index label 0 has dpd = 0. What does the second line do?
quiz.code:
late = loans[loans["dpd"] > 0]
late.loc[0]
options: Returns an empty Series
Returns the first late loan
Returns loan 0 anyway
Raises KeyError — label 0 is not in late
quiz.explain: loc selects by label, iloc by position; after a filter they differ — late.iloc[0] is 'the first late loan' (→ section 1, 'loc and iloc').

quiz.q: This line raises an error. What is the fix?
quiz.code: loans[loans["dpd"] > 0 & loans["status"] == "active"]
options: Write and instead of &
Put brackets around each condition: (loans["dpd"] > 0) & (loans["status"] == "active")
Convert dpd to int first
Use loans.iloc instead
quiz.explain: & binds tighter than > and ==, so every condition needs its own brackets; and / or do not work on a whole Series (→ section 1, 'Selecting rows').

quiz.q: What happens to the 7 429 loans with dpd = 0?
quiz.code: pd.cut(loans["dpd"], bins=[0, 30, 60, 90, np.inf])
options: pd.cut raises an error
They become NaN — intervals are right-closed, and (0, 30] does not contain 0
They land in (0, 30]
pd.cut creates a '0' bucket for them
quiz.explain: The first edge must be below the smallest value (-1 for DPD); np.inf closes the top (→ section 1, 'pd.cut').

quiz.q: On loans_status.csv, what does this give, in % with two decimals?
quiz.code: 100 * loans.loc[loans["dpd"] > 30, "outstanding"].sum() / loans["outstanding"].sum()
quiz.explain: Outstanding of loans with dpd > 30 ÷ total outstanding = 6.51 bn of 208.7 bn = PAR30 (→ Company corner).

quiz.q: Which statements about missing values in pandas are true?
options: fillna(0) on monthly_income gives a lower, wrong mean
mean() skips NaN, like SQL's AVG
dropna() without subset= drops a row if any column is missing
col == np.nan finds the missing rows
count() counts every row, NaN included
quiz.explain: NaN is pandas' NULL: aggregates skip it, == never finds it (use isna()), and fillna(0) on an income is a decision that invents zero earners (→ section 1, 'Missing values').

quiz.q: You count September applications on applied_at, which holds a date and a time. Which filter is right?
options: applied_at.dt.month == 9
quiz.explain: between is inclusive and "2026-09-30" means midnight, so the 30th's afternoon is lost; dt.month == 9 also catches September 2025. Half-open, always (→ section 1, 'Selecting rows', P5).

quiz.q: portfolio_summary counts 3 030 loans disbursed in 2026; week 4's tile said 3 051. Why?
options: parse_dates shifts every date by a day
The function uses < AS_OF, so the 21 loans disbursed on 1 October itself are out
pandas drops rows with NaN dates
Week 4 counted duplicate loans
quiz.explain: Half-open < AS_OF excludes the as-of day; neither convention is wrong, but the docstring must say which (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Company corner: what is the numerator of PAR30?
options: The whole outstanding of loans with dpd > 30
The number of loans with dpd > 30
The outstanding of loans in the 31-60 bucket only
The overdue instalments of loans more than 30 days late
quiz.explain: A 500 m loan one day past 30 puts the full 500 m into PAR30; overdue ÷ outstanding is the arrears ratio and the count share is another number (→ Company corner).

w05d3.t: Week 5 · Day 3 — pandas II: groupby, merge and the cleaning pipeline

quiz.q: You need each payment's share of its loan's total, on every payment row. Which call gives the loan total per row?
options: pay.pivot_table(index="loan_id", values="amount")
pay.groupby("loan_id")["amount"].transform("sum")
pay.groupby("loan_id")["amount"].agg("sum")
pay["amount"].sum()
quiz.explain: agg returns one row per group; transform returns one value per original row — the window function SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY) (→ section 1, 'transform').

quiz.q: You expected len(m) == 92 193. Why is it smaller?
quiz.code:
m = inst.merge(paid, on="installment_id")
len(inst), len(m)
options: merge defaults to how="inner", so instalments with no payment vanish
paid has duplicate installment_ids
installment_id is text in one of the tables
merge drops rows with NaN in any column
quiz.explain: The default join is inner; use how="left", fillna(0) after the merge, and assert len(m) == len(inst) (→ section 1, 'merge', P6).

quiz.q: inst has 10 instalments; paid has one row for each of the 6 instalments that received a payment. How many rows does m have?
quiz.code:
m = inst.merge(paid, on="installment_id")
len(m)
quiz.explain: The default join is inner: only instalments with a payment survive, and the 4 without a payment — exactly the ones DPD needs — vanish; how="left" keeps all 10 (→ section 1, 'merge').

quiz.q: installments.merge(payments_raw, on="installment_id", validate="1:1") raises MergeError on the raw payments file. What does it tell you?
options: pandas cannot validate more than 50 000 rows
The merge must be rewritten as a loop
Some instalments have more than one payment row (here the duplicate payments), so payments to instalments is m:1 — the grain you stated was wrong
installment_id has NaN values
quiz.explain: validate turns a wrong belief about the grain into an error before any number is wrong — the week-2 fan-out, caught (→ section 1, 'validate= and indicator=', P8).

quiz.q: Which statements about duplicated / drop_duplicates are true?
options: Without subset= it compares all columns, and finds 0 payment duplicates because payment_id differs
subset= defines what 'the same' means
drop_duplicates keeps the first row in the current order, so sort first
duplicated(keep=False) marks every member of a duplicate group
It always keeps the row with the lowest id, whatever the order
quiz.explain: The key defines sameness, the sort defines the survivor, the assert proves both (→ section 1, 'Duplicates').

quiz.q: pd.to_datetime(birth_date, errors="coerce") produces 0 NaT. Are the birth dates clean?
options: Yes, if the dtype is datetime64
No — parsing is syntax; 2031-04-12 parses fine and still breaks the business rule
No — coerce silently turns bad dates into 1900-01-01
Yes — every value parsed
quiz.explain: Validity is a rule you write (not in the future, not before 1920); flag and blank with .where, never guess a date (→ section 1, 'Dates that lie').

quiz.q: What does the concat produce?
quiz.code:
a = pay[pay["region"] == "Tashkent"]
b = pay[pay["region"] != "Tashkent"].rename(columns={"amount": "Amount"})
pd.concat([a, b])
options: All rows and one column more: amount is NaN in b's rows, Amount is NaN in a's
An error: the column names differ
Only the columns both frames share
One amount column — pandas ignores case
quiz.explain: concat matches columns by name, without an error; assert set(a.columns) == set(b.columns) before every concat (→ section 1, 'concat', P9).

quiz.q: Company corner: in the DPD function, a late loan's DPD is…
options: as-of − the due date of its oldest matured instalment that is not fully paid
as-of − the disbursement date
the number of unpaid instalments × 30
as-of − the due date of its most recent unpaid instalment
quiz.explain: Per loan: AS_OF − min(due_date) over instalments that are matured and not fully paid; 0 when nothing is late (→ Company corner).

w05d4.t: Week 5 · Day 4 — Charts and the SQL bridge: matplotlib, seaborn, read_sql

quiz.q: Why does the figure pack use fig, ax = plt.subplots() instead of plt.plot()?
options: Every title, label and formatter then belongs to a named chart — clear and safe when there are several
plt.plot cannot draw lines
Only a fig can be saved to PNG
subplots draws faster
quiz.explain: plt.plot draws on 'the current axes', which gets confusing with several charts; the object interface makes the chart yours (→ section 1, 'Figure and axes').

quiz.q: Each bar is meant to be the product's total outstanding. What does it show?
quiz.code: sns.barplot(data=loans, x="outstanding", y="product")
options: The mean outstanding per loan of each product
The number of loans
The total
The median
quiz.explain: seaborn's barplot aggregates with the mean by default — pass estimator=sum or aggregate first (→ section 1, 'seaborn').

quiz.q: sns.heatmap of a vintage matrix (cohort × MOB) needs which shape of data?
options: A Series of percentages
Wide: a pivot with cohorts as rows and MOB as columns
Any shape
Long: one row per cohort × MOB
quiz.explain: hue-based charts want long data (melt); heatmap wants a wide matrix (pivot) — most 'seaborn does not work' moments are the wrong shape (→ section 1, 'seaborn').

quiz.q: Both lines return the same count today. Which one belongs in the figure pack?
quiz.code:
as_of = "2026-10-01"
q1 = pd.read_sql(f"SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM payments WHERE paid_at > '{as_of}'", con)
q2 = pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM payments WHERE paid_at > ?", con, params=(as_of,))
options: Neither — read the whole table and filter in pandas
Either — they are identical
q1 — easier to read
q2 — params= passes the value safely; an f-string breaks on a quote and invites injection on a real server
quiz.explain: Values go in params=, never into the SQL text (→ section 1, 'read_sql', P11).

quiz.q: On nur.db, what number does this query return?
quiz.code: pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM payments WHERE paid_at > ?", con, params=("2026-10-01",))
quiz.explain: 24 forward-dated payments (53.4 m) — the rows every payment sum excludes with paid_at <= AS_OF (→ section 1, 'read_sql').

quiz.q: Which of these are chart rules, not matters of taste?
options: No legend for a single series
A log axis on a bar chart so small values show
A second y-axis so two lines fit
Drop the one-day October point from a time series
Bars start at zero
The title states the finding
quiz.explain: A log axis breaks 'bars from zero', and two y-axes invent crossings; the October point (one day) reads as a crash (→ section 1, 'What chart for what question').

quiz.q: Figure 2's title says "208.7 bn". Next month the total changes. What is the lasting fix?
options: Add a footnote with the date
Build the title from the data with an f-string
Edit the title by hand each month
Remove all numbers from titles
quiz.explain: A title computed from the data cannot go stale; an assert above the chart catches a changed extract (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Company corner: what makes the figure pack Timur's and not a favour?
options: One AS_OF used in every query, titles computed from the data, an assert before each chart — then Restart & Run All
Five charts on one 2 × 2 grid
Hand-picked colours each month
Saving every chart as SVG
quiz.explain: Reproducibility is the deliverable: change AS_OF, run all, five new files (→ Company corner).

w05d5.t: Week 5 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: the EDA report, in pandas

quiz.q: Every yoy_pct value comes out NaN. Why?
quiz.code:
m26 = m.loc["2026-01":]
m26["yoy_pct"] = m26["disbursed"].pct_change(12) * 100
options: rolling(3) must run first
pct_change needs dates as text
The frame was cut to 2026 before pct_change(12), so no row is 12 months back
pct_change works only on integers
quiz.explain: Compute on the full 33-month frame and filter for display afterwards — week 3's LAG trap in a new spelling (→ S7).

quiz.q: Where are the loans whose customer has no income?
quiz.code:
lc["band"] = pd.cut(lc["monthly_income"], [0, 5e6, 10e6, 20e6, np.inf], right=False)
pd.crosstab(lc["band"], lc["risk_grade"])
options: In the <5m row
In a row called NaN
pd.cut raises an error on NaN
Nowhere — the NaN band is dropped from the crosstab silently
quiz.explain: Turn the NaN band into a row (astype(str).replace("nan", "unknown")) — the week-2 NULL-band lesson (→ S10).

quiz.q: Why right=False in the income cut?
options: pd.cut requires it for money
It makes the cut faster
It keeps NaN as a band
So that [5m, 10m) matches SQL's WHEN monthly_income < 10000000 — a customer earning exactly 5 000 000 stays in the same band as in week 3
quiz.explain: pd.cut is right-closed by default; the SQL rule was '<', so right=False reproduces it (→ S10).

quiz.q: Summing principal after merging instalments onto loans gives ×24.7. Which merge argument would have stopped it?
options: indicator=True
how="left"
sort=False
validate= with the grain you expect (e.g. "m:1")
quiz.explain: validate raises MergeError when a key is not unique where you promised — the week-2 fan-out becomes an error (→ 'Common mistakes').

quiz.q: You forgot parse_dates=, yet L["disbursed_at"].max() still returns a value. What is wrong?
options: Nothing
It is a string comparison that works on ISO text by luck; .dt and date arithmetic are unavailable
max() returned NaN
pandas converted the column automatically
quiz.explain: parse_dates= is where the typing happens; without it .max() compares text and still 'works' (→ S3).

quiz.q: Which belong in every checkpoint section?
options: The week-3 number next to yours — an assert where it must be exact, a printed pair where rounding may differ
One finding Bekzod can read aloud
The grain in a comment
Thirty cells showing every attempt
A match / mismatch line that says why
quiz.explain: Three cells per section, not thirty: the reviewer reads the finding, checks the match line, then the output (→ 'Working method').

quiz.q: Which Jupyter command proves the notebook is reproducible before you submit? (Kernel → …)
quiz.explain: Restart & Run All runs every cell from a clean kernel; then save, so the outputs are inside the file (→ 'Rules').

quiz.q: Your pandas number differs from week 3 and the line under it explains why (half-open vs inclusive filter). What does it cost?
options: Half the section's points
Nothing — only an unexplained mismatch costs the number points
The finding points
The whole section
quiz.explain: A mismatch is not a failure if the line under it says why (→ 'Working method').

w05d6.t: Week 5 · Day 6 — Section exam: Python and pandas (Week 5)

quiz.q: The principal was read from a CSV file as text. What does this print?
quiz.code:
principal = "31150000"
print(principal * 2)
options: A TypeError
quiz.explain: Text times 2 repeats the text. Convert first: int(principal) * 2 gives 62300000. Everything read from a CSV is text until you convert it (→ Week 5 · Day 1, Values and types).

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.explain: Positions start at 0, and a slice x[a:b] stops before b. So x[1:4] is 20, 30 and 40, and their sum is 90. x[5] would be an IndexError (→ Week 5 · Day 1, Lists).

quiz.q: What happens on the last line?
quiz.code:
def total(a, b):
    print(a + b)

r = total(2, 3)
r + 1
options: It returns 6
A TypeError: total() printed the answer but returned None
It returns 5
A NameError
quiz.explain: A function without return gives back None. A function that only prints looks right on the screen and is useless to the next line of code (→ Week 5 · Day 1, Functions).

quiz.q: What does bucket(7) return?
quiz.explain: The first true test wins, and 7 <= 60 is true before the 30 is ever looked at. Write the tests from the smallest edge up: 30, then 60 (→ Week 5 · Day 1, if / elif / else).

quiz.q: Which line returns the active loans that are late?
options: loans[loans["dpd"] > 0 and loans["status"] == "active"]
loans[loans["dpd"] > 0 & loans["status"] == "active"]
loans[(loans["dpd"] > 0) & (loans["status"] == "active")]
loans["dpd" > 0, "status" == "active"]
quiz.explain: Use & | ~ between masks, never and / or / not, and put brackets round every condition, because & binds tighter than > and ==. Without brackets the line fails or silently builds the wrong mask (→ Week 5 · Day 2, Selecting rows).

quiz.q: What does this line do to loans?
quiz.code: loans[loans["dpd"] > 90]["flag"] = 1
options: It adds a column flag, set to 1 for the loans over 90 days late
Nothing: the assignment lands on a temporary copy, and pandas only warns
It deletes the loans over 90 days late
It raises a KeyError
quiz.explain: Chained indexing (two brackets in a row) writes into a copy. Assign through .loc: loans.loc[loans["dpd"] > 90, "flag"] = 1 (→ Week 5 · Day 2, New columns).

quiz.q: 7 429 loans have dpd = 0. You bucket the column like this. Which rows become NaN?
options: None
The 7 429 loans with dpd = 0: the first interval is (0, 30], which does not contain 0
The loans with dpd above 90
The loans with dpd exactly 30
quiz.explain: Intervals are closed on the right by default, and the first edge must be below the smallest value. Start at -1, or the whole current book disappears into NaN (→ Week 5 · Day 2, pd.cut).

quiz.q: You merge the instalments with their payments, and the forgotten how= leaves the default. What is lost?
quiz.code: inst.merge(pay, on="installment_id")
options: Nothing: the default is a left join
The instalments with no payment, the unpaid ones that DPD is about: the default is an inner join
The payments with no instalment
Nothing, but the key is renamed
quiz.explain: pandas merges with how="inner", not "left" as many SQL readers expect. Write how= on every merge and count the rows after it (→ Week 5 · Day 3, merge).

quiz.q: A payment can have several rows per installment_id. What happens here?
quiz.code: inst.merge(pay, on="installment_id", how="left", validate="one_to_one")
options: Pandas raises a MergeError: you declared the grain, and the data disagrees
Pandas keeps the first payment of each installment
Pandas sums the payments
Nothing: validate is ignored on a left join
quiz.explain: validate= costs nothing: a duplicate key on the right would multiply rows and make every later sum too big, with no error. A MergeError is a free lesson about the grain (→ Week 5 · Day 3, validate= and indicator=).

quiz.q: Which pandas method is the equivalent of SQL's GROUP BY? Type its name.
quiz.explain: df.groupby("product")["outstanding"].sum() is SELECT product, SUM(outstanding) … GROUP BY product. It drops the rows whose key is NaN unless you pass dropna=False (→ Week 5 · Day 3, groupby; Day 2, SQL ↔ pandas).

quiz.q: Which statements about missing values in pandas are true?
options: isna() finds blanks; == np.nan never does
fillna(0) on an income column gives a confident, wrong mean
dropna() with no subset= drops a row when any column is blank
value_counts() shows the NaN row by default
A whole-number column with one blank becomes float64
quiz.explain: NaN is not equal to anything, itself included. value_counts() hides NaN unless you pass dropna=False, so the shares are shares of the non-blank rows. Check dtypes before you trust a column (→ Week 5 · Day 2, Missing values; value_counts).

quiz.q: What does the new column t contain?
quiz.code: pay["t"] = pay.groupby("loan_id")["amount"].sum()
options: The loan's total, repeated on every payment row of that loan
NaN or another loan's total on most rows: the result is aligned on the index, not repeated per row
The sum of all payments in the table
An error
quiz.explain: An aggregate has one row per group, and pandas aligns it with the frame by index label. For a per-row value use transform: pay.groupby("loan_id")["amount"].transform("sum") (→ Week 5 · Day 3, transform).

quiz.q: You clean dates with pd.to_datetime(col, errors="coerce"). The file still holds 2031-04-12 as a disbursement date, and the as-of date is 2026-10-01. What is true?
options: coerce catches it and turns it into NaT
coerce fixes unparseable text like "n/a" and "31.02.2026", but 2031-04-12 is a valid date and passes: the business rule is yours to write
to_datetime raises an error for dates after the as-of date
The date is moved to 2026-10-01
quiz.explain: Parsing is syntax; validity is a rule. Write the check yourself (for example df["disbursed_at"] > as_of), count the rows it finds, and put the count in an assert (→ Week 5 · Day 3, Dates that lie).

quiz.q: payments has 52 875 rows and payment_id is different on every row. How many rows does payments.drop_duplicates() remove?
quiz.explain: Without subset=, pandas compares all columns, and payment_id never repeats, so nothing is a duplicate. The 25 real repeats need subset=["installment_id", "paid_at", "amount"] and a sort first, so the right row survives (→ Week 5 · Day 3, Duplicates).

quiz.q: You draw outstanding by product with seaborn on the raw loan rows and no estimator. SME's bar shows 161 m instead of 125.9 bn. Why?
quiz.code: sns.barplot(data=loans, x="product", y="outstanding")
options: sns.barplot draws the mean per category by default: it shows the average outstanding per loan, not the total
The y-axis is in millions
seaborn drops the largest loans
The chart needs tight_layout()
quiz.explain: barplot summarises with the mean. For a total pass estimator=sum, or aggregate with groupby first and draw the result (→ Week 5 · Day 4, seaborn).

quiz.q: Which way of passing a date into a query is right?
options: pd.read_sql(f"SELECT * FROM payments WHERE paid_at > '{as_of}'", con)
pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM payments WHERE paid_at > ?", con, params=[as_of])
pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM payments WHERE paid_at > " + as_of, con)
pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM payments WHERE paid_at > as_of", con)
quiz.explain: Values go in params=, never into the SQL text. An f-string works today and breaks on the first value with a quote in it; on a real server it is how an injection gets in (→ Week 5 · Day 4, sqlite3 and read_sql).

quiz.q: Query A returns the product codes MICRO, CONS and BNPL. Query B returns CONS, SME and AUTO. How many rows does A UNION B return?
quiz.explain: UNION removes duplicates: CONS appears once, so 5 rows. UNION ALL keeps every row and returns 6. Use UNION ALL when the blocks cannot overlap, or when you want every row (→ Week 2 · Day 2, Set operators).

quiz.q: Bekzod asks for the five biggest loans. What is wrong with this query?
quiz.code: SELECT loan_id, principal FROM loans LIMIT 5;
options: Nothing: LIMIT 5 returns the five biggest
LIMIT without ORDER BY returns some five rows, not the biggest: sort first (ORDER BY principal DESC), then cut
LIMIT cannot be used on loans
It must be TOP 5 in SQLite
quiz.explain: Sort first, then cut. SQL Server writes SELECT TOP 5 … ORDER BY principal DESC; SQLite writes … ORDER BY principal DESC LIMIT 5 (→ Week 1 · Day 2, LIMIT and TOP).

quiz.q: The method column holds the values 'Card', 'card', 'card ' (with a space) and 'cash'. How many rows does this query return?
quiz.code:
SELECT method, COUNT(*) FROM payments
GROUP BY method;
quiz.explain: GROUP BY groups exact values, so 'Card', 'card' and 'card ' are three groups, plus 'cash'. Look at the labels of every grouped result before you trust its counts, or clean with LOWER(TRIM(method)) (→ Week 2 · Day 2, GROUP BY; Day 3, TRIM).

quiz.q: What does this query return?
quiz.code:
SELECT loan_id FROM loans l
WHERE principal > (SELECT AVG(x.principal)
                   FROM loans x
                   WHERE x.product_id = l.product_id);
options: The loans bigger than the average of the whole table
The loans bigger than the average of their own product: the inner query reads the outer row
One row, the average
An error: the subquery returns many rows
quiz.explain: The inner query uses l.product_id from the outer row, so conceptually it runs once per loan: this is a correlated subquery. The aliases l and x must differ (→ Week 3 · Day 3, Correlated subquery).

quiz.q: These two statements run one after the other. What happens with the second?
options: It works: big stays available
An error, no such table: a CTE lives for one statement only; reuse needs a view or a table
It returns NULL
It returns the maximum of the whole loans table
quiz.explain: A CTE exists for the single statement right after the WITH. To reuse a result across queries, create a view or a table (→ Week 3 · Day 3, CTE; Day 4, What a view is).

quiz.q: tblLoans is filtered to the active loans. What do these two cells show?
quiz.code:
=SUM(tblLoans[outstanding])
=SUBTOTAL(109, tblLoans[outstanding])
options: The same number
SUM adds every row of the Table, filtered out or not; SUBTOTAL(109, …) adds only the visible rows
SUM adds the visible rows; SUBTOTAL adds all
Both show #VALUE!
quiz.explain: SUM ignores filters; the status bar and SUBTOTAL(109, …) respect them. Read numbers from formulas, and know which of the two you are looking at (→ Week 4 · Day 1, SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT).

quiz.q: You tick all columns in Remove Duplicates on payments_dirty (payment_id is different on every row). How many rows does Excel remove?
quiz.explain: A duplicate agrees on what matters, not on everything. With payment_id ticked, no two rows are equal. Define sameness on installment_id + paid_at + amount, and count the groups with COUNTIFS before you remove anything (→ Week 4 · Day 3, Remove Duplicates).

quiz.q: Which Excel function adds a column for the rows that meet several conditions? Type its name.
quiz.explain: SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criterion1, …): every pair is one more AND. It is SQL's SUM with a WHERE. In a Russian Excel it is СУММЕСЛИМН (→ Week 4 · Day 1, COUNTIFS, SUMIFS, AVERAGEIFS).

quiz.q: A conditional-formatting rule must colour a whole row by the bucket in column M, starting at row 2. Which formula?
quiz.explain: Pin the column, free the row: $M2. With $M$2 every row is coloured by row 2's bucket; with M2 the rule drifts one column right in every cell (→ Week 4 · Day 2, Conditional formatting).

w06d1.t: Week 6 · Day 1 — Probability and distributions: how random is a default?

quiz.q: 45.1 % of all FPDs came through the app. What is the FPD rate of an app loan?
options: 1.70 % — P(FPD | app) = 41 / 2 411, a different denominator
quiz.explain: P(app | FPD) answers 'where do defaults come from'; P(FPD | app) answers 'how risky is an app loan' (→ section 1, 'Conditional probability').

quiz.q: What does the second line return?
quiz.code:
X = stats.binom(400, 91 / 7099)
X.sf(10)
quiz.explain: sf(k) is P(X > k); 'k or more' is sf(k − 1) — the off-by-one of the day (→ section 1, 'Bernoulli and binomial').

quiz.q: A rule catches 95 % of frauds and flags 2 % of honest applicants; fraud is 0.5 % of applications. What share of flagged applications are fraud, in %?
quiz.explain: 0.95 × 0.005 / (0.95 × 0.005 + 0.02 × 0.995) = 19.3 %: four flags in five are honest people — the base-rate trap (→ section 1, 'Bayes').

quiz.q: Which statements describe the Poisson distribution?
options: If arrivals are Poisson, the gaps between them are exponential
Its mean equals its variance (λ)
It can never exceed a fixed n
It is a symmetric bell for any λ
It counts events in a fixed window arriving independently at a constant rate
quiz.explain: Applications per hour: λ = 1.44, variance 1.44 — the Poisson fingerprint; the minutes between them are exponential (→ section 1, 'Poisson', 'Exponential').

quiz.q: For 400 independent loans the expected total loss grows like n. Its standard deviation grows like…
options: n
it stays the same
n²
√n
quiz.explain: Variances add, so the sd grows like √n — the total becomes relatively steadier, which is why a lender wants many small loans (→ section 1, 'Random variables').

quiz.q: A normal fitted to approved loans' scores puts 6.2 % below 600; the data say 4.3 %. Why?
options: The approval rule cut the left tail — a selected sample is not the applicant population
Too few loans
The sd used ddof=0
Scores follow a Poisson
quiz.explain: Applicants' scores are close to normal; approved loans are a selection, and every model fitted on them inherits that (→ section 1, 'Normal').

quiz.q: A reviewer re-runs your cell and gets 3.61 % instead of your 3.55 %. What is missing?
quiz.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng()
months = rng.binomial(400, 91 / 7099, size=100_000)
np.mean(months >= 10)
options: A seed: np.random.default_rng(2026)
>= should be >
size must be at least 1 000 000
months must be floats
quiz.explain: An unseeded simulation gives different numbers on every run; seed it, and check it against the formula where one exists (→ section 1, 'Simulation').

quiz.q: Company corner: why is the crude EL table's 'PD' a teaching simplification?
options: It uses 90+ instead of 30+
LGD should be 100 %
It is a share of loans now 90+ that mixes loans of every age — a loan disbursed last month had no time to default — so it is neither a 12-month nor a lifetime PD
EAD should be the original principal
quiz.explain: Real PDs come from scorecards and vintage / roll-rate models on a fixed horizon; the 60 % LGD is a guess too (→ Company corner).

w06d2.t: Week 6 · Day 2 — Samples, the CLT and confidence intervals

quiz.q: App FPD: 95 % CI 1.26–2.30 %. Which reading is correct?
options: There is a 95 % probability the true app rate is between 1.26 and 2.30 %
95 % of app loans have an FPD rate in that range
The procedure captures the true rate in 95 % of repeated samples; this interval either contains it or not
If two channels' intervals overlap, the channels do not differ
quiz.explain: 95 % is a property of the procedure; the true rate is fixed, and overlap is not a test (→ section 1, 'What 95 % means').

quiz.q: Why Wilson rather than Wald for an FPD rate near 1.28 % on a branch-month of 400 loans?
options: Near 0 % a rate's sampling distribution is skewed: a '95 %' Wald covers about 88 %, can go negative and collapses to zero width at 0 events
Wald needs a seed
Wilson works only for very large n
Wilson is always narrower
quiz.explain: Wilson inverts the score test: never negative, asymmetric the right way, close to 95 % coverage (→ section 1, 'The Wilson interval').

quiz.q: Which line makes this interval slightly too narrow?
quiz.code:
m = smp.mean()                                  # line 1
s = np.std(smp)                                 # line 2
se = s / np.sqrt(len(smp))                      # line 3
stats.t.interval(0.95, len(smp) - 1, loc=m, scale=se)   # line 4
options: line 1
line 2 — numpy's std defaults to ddof=0, the population formula
line 3
line 4 — a z value is needed instead of t
quiz.explain: A sample interval needs ddof=1 (pandas' .std() already uses it; numpy does not) (→ Mistakes, section 1 'A good estimate').

quiz.q: How many first instalments do you need to estimate a rate near p = 91 / 7 099 to within ±0.5 points at 95 %? (n = z² p(1 − p) / E², round up)
quiz.explain: 1.96² × 0.01282 × 0.98718 / 0.005² ≈ 1 945; for ±0.25 points it is four times as many (→ section 1, 'Sample size for a given margin', P13).

quiz.q: Which statements about the bootstrap are true?
options: With 5 events it is reliable for a rate near 0 %
It resamples the sample with replacement
It needs normally distributed data
It gives an interval for a median or a ratio of sums, where no SE formula exists
Seed it so a reviewer gets your interval
quiz.explain: It can only reshuffle what it saw, so with few events it is too narrow — Wilson for rates near zero, bootstrap for medians and ratios (→ section 1, 'The bootstrap').

quiz.q: To halve the standard error of an estimate, the sample size must be…
options: squared
halved
doubled
quadrupled
quiz.explain: SE = s / √n, so halving it needs four times the n (→ section 1, 'Standard error').

quiz.q: By hand, Wald gives −0.50 % to 3.17 % for 2 FPDs in 150 loans. What goes on the dashboard?
quiz.code: proportion_confint(2, 150, method="normal")   # Wald
options: Wilson, about 0.37–4.73 %: never negative and close to 95 % coverage
Wald as statsmodels prints it (clipped to 0–3.17 %)
No interval — 150 loans is too few
Only the rate, 1.33 %
quiz.explain: statsmodels clips the Wald limit and hides the problem; Wilson says honestly 'between almost nothing and about 5 %' (→ P10).

quiz.q: Company corner: Bukhara has the highest FPD30 of ten branches (14 / 586). What should the risk pack do?
options: Show the rate with n and its Wilson interval and compare it with the funnel limits for its size; watch it rather than punish it
Report the rate without n — n confuses readers
Rank the branches and act on the worst
Drop Bukhara from the book rate
quiz.explain: A league table guarantees a 'worst branch' even when all are equal; a funnel flags by size-adjusted limits, not by rank (→ Company corner).

w06d3.t: Week 6 · Day 3 — Hypothesis tests I: is the difference real?

quiz.q: Which is the definition of a p-value?
options: The probability, computed assuming H₀ is true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed
The probability that H₀ is true
The size of the difference
The probability that the result is due to chance
quiz.explain: It is computed assuming H₀, so it cannot be H₀'s probability, and it says nothing about size (→ section 1, 'The p-value').

quiz.q: App vs branch: z-test p = 0.032; the three-channel χ² gives p = 0.078. What is going on?
options: Different questions: χ² asks whether the three channels differ at all; the z-test asks about the two extremes, a pair chosen after seeing the table
The z-test used the wrong n
A contradiction — one of the tests is wrong
χ² is always less powerful, so ignore it
quiz.explain: That is why the committee note calls the evidence moderate (→ section 1, 'Chi-square', P9).

quiz.q: w holds the FPD30 % of the same ten branches in 2025 and 2026. Which test should replace this one?
quiz.code: stats.ttest_ind(w[2026], w[2025])
options: stats.fisher_exact
A chi-square test
stats.ttest_rel — the same branches measured twice, so the test works on the differences
Welch: equal_var=False
quiz.explain: Pairing removes the between-branch spread: p = 0.031 paired vs 0.055 unpaired (→ section 1, 'Paired vs independent').

quiz.q: A 2 × 2 χ² without continuity correction equals z². If z = 2.147, what is χ² (two decimals)?
quiz.explain: 2.147² = 4.61 and the p-value is identical (0.0318); scipy's default Yates correction gives 4.12, p = 0.042 (→ section 1, 'Chi-square', P11).

quiz.q: Which are good practice when reporting a test?
options: Read p = 0.078 as 'FPD does not depend on channel'
Write p < 0.001, never p = 0.000
Report the effect size with its CI next to the p-value
Test at the loan level when loans are the units, not at the payment level
Switch to a one-sided test after seeing which group is higher
quiz.explain: Switching sides after looking is p-hacking, and p > 0.05 is absence of evidence (→ Mistakes, section 1 'Effect size').

quiz.q: Late payment, grade A vs B: z = −15.45 on payments, −11.59 on loans. Why so different?
options: A loan contributes about seven payments that are not independent, so the payment-level test pretends to have more information and inflates z
The loan test used Welch
Loans were counted twice
Payments are more accurate
quiz.explain: Test at the unit that was sampled — the loan; on a borderline question the wrong grain manufactures significance (→ P12).

quiz.q: Welch on principal by channel gives t = −43, p ≈ 0. What can you conclude about channels?
quiz.code:
pd.crosstab(loans.channel, loans.product_id)
# app -> 1 (MICRO) only · partner -> 3 (BNPL) only · branch -> 2, 4, 5 (CONS, AUTO, SME)
options: A one-sided test is needed
Nothing about channels: channel and product are confounded, and no test separates them
App customers borrow less because of the app
Variances must be equal first
quiz.explain: App = Micro only, partner = BNPL only; Nilufar's FPD gap is also, inevitably, a product gap (→ section 1, 'Two-sample t-test').

quiz.q: Company corner: which sentence must NOT appear in the risk-committee note?
options: App loans: +6.6 FPDs per 1 000 (RR 1.63, CI 1.04–2.56)
Keep the channel; run a reminder test and re-test on Q4 vintages
FPD30 = first instalment not fully paid within 30 days of its due date
Partner is proven no different from branch (p = 0.80)
quiz.explain: p = 0.80 is absence of evidence, not proof of no difference (→ Company corner).

w06d4.t: Week 6 · Day 4 — Hypothesis tests II: non-parametric tests, multiple comparisons and power

quiz.q: On the same Auto vs SME days late, Welch gives p = 0.02 and Mann–Whitney p = 0.32. Which is wrong?
options: Mann–Whitney — it ignores the tail
Welch — the data are skewed
Both — run a third test
Neither: Welch asks about the average days late, Mann–Whitney whether a typical payment is later
quiz.explain: Decide which question the business asks before choosing the test, never run both and quote the smaller p (→ section 1, 'When the t-test is wrong', P2).

quiz.q: What does the Mann–Whitney U test compare?
options: The means
The medians
The variances
Whether a random value from one group tends to be larger than one from the other — under H₀, P(X > Y) = ½
quiz.explain: It works on ranks and compares whole distributions; equal medians can still differ (→ section 1, 'Mann–Whitney U').

quiz.q: Which test do you report for this table?
quiz.code:
t = [[4, 63], [2, 177]]          # partner vs branch, FPD / no FPD
stats.chi2_contingency(t)[3]      # expected [[1.63, 65.37], [4.37, 174.63]]
options: χ² without correction (p = 0.028)
A t-test on the two rates
Fisher's exact test — two expected counts are below 5
χ² with Yates (p = 0.083)
quiz.explain: χ² is an approximation that needs expected counts ≥ 5; Fisher is exact at any n (→ section 1, 'Chi-square or Fisher', P7).

quiz.q: You run 10 independent tests at α = 5 % and nothing is real. What is the chance of at least one false alarm, in %?
quiz.explain: 1 − 0.95¹⁰ = 40.1 % — the family-wise error rate; Holm or Bonferroni bring it back to 5 % (→ section 1, 'Multiple comparisons').

quiz.q: What does this return?
quiz.code: multipletests([0.0318, 0.153, 0.804], method="holm")[1]
quiz.explain: Holm: the smallest × 3, the next × 2, the last × 1, keeping the running maximum; [0.0954, 0.459, 1.0] is Bonferroni (→ P8).

quiz.q: Power depends on…
options: α
the noise — for a rate, how close it is to 0 %
the p-value you observed
n
the seed of the simulation
the effect size
quiz.explain: Power is fixed before the data: α, effect, n and variability; rare outcomes like FPD are expensive to test (→ section 1, 'Power and sample size').

quiz.q: You look at a running experiment every month and stop at the first p < 0.05. What happens to the 5 % false-positive rate?
options: It grows: in the simulation one look gave 5 %, monthly looks about 21 %
It falls, because you stop earlier
It becomes exactly 10 %
Nothing — each look is a 5 % test
quiz.explain: Each look is another test; fix the sample size and the end date in advance, or use a sequential design (→ section 1, 'Peeking').

quiz.q: Company corner: the 2 000-loan SMS test has 9 % power for FPD 1.28 → 1.00 %. What would a 'not significant' result mean?
options: Almost nothing — the test would miss a real effect 91 % of the time; change the metric (first instalment paid late) or decide on cost
Run it again with 2 000 more loans and it will be significant
The SMS does not work
FPD rose
quiz.explain: Never read a null result from an underpowered test as 'no effect' (→ Company corner).

w06d5.t: Week 6 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: intervals and the test-choice quiz

quiz.q: Which gives the sample standard deviation (ddof = 1) for a t interval?
quiz.code: v = loans.loc[loans["code"] == "AUTO", "principal"].astype(float)   # a pandas Series
options: np.sqrt(np.var(v))
np.std(v)
v.std(ddof=0)
v.std()
quiz.explain: pandas' .std() defaults to ddof=1; numpy's np.std and np.var default to ddof=0 — the deduction seen most often in A1 (→ A1, Day 2).

quiz.q: Which interval does this return?
quiz.code:
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint
proportion_confint(41, 2411)
options: Clopper–Pearson
Wilson
A bootstrap interval
Wald — method="normal" is the default; pass method="wilson"
quiz.explain: statsmodels' default is the Wald interval; a rate near 0 % needs method="wilson" (→ Day 2, A2 deductions).

quiz.q: The average Micro ticket is 2.71 m; one Micro loan is 4.99 m. What do you do before calling it an outlier?
options: Replace it with the mean
Run Shapiro–Wilk
Delete it — it is far from the mean
Look at the spread (z ≈ 1.7) and find out what it is: 4.99 m is just under the product limit
quiz.explain: Never delete by a z-score alone; a limit, a data error and a real large loan need different treatment (→ Warm-up 1).

quiz.q: Shapiro–Wilk on 500 app principals gives p ≈ 10⁻¹². Does that forbid a t-test on the mean of all 2 669 app principals?
options: Yes, unless you take logs
Yes — the data are not normal
Only if Levene also rejects
No — the t-test needs the sample mean to be approximately normal, which the CLT gives at n = 2 669
quiz.explain: Normality of the statistic, not of the data (→ Warm-up 3, Day 3 'Checking assumptions').

quiz.q: Applicants' scores: μ = 659.6, σ = 59.5. What is the z-score of a score of 780 (two decimals)?
quiz.explain: z = (780 − 659.6) / 59.5 = 2.02, so the normal model puts about 2.2 % at 780 or above (→ Warm-up 2).

quiz.q: Which belong in every Part A interpretation?
options: What someone should do — or not do — with it
An effect size next to any p-value
"H₀ is rejected" without saying which hypothesis, in business words
The number with its uncertainty (interval or p-value) and the method named
quiz.explain: Two sentences: the number with its test, then the decision it supports; a correct number with no interpretation earns 6 of 10 (→ 'What every Part A answer contains').

quiz.q: A test gives p = 0.051. What do you report?
options: 'No effect'
Switch to a one-sided test
Re-run until p < 0.05
Nothing magical happens at 0.05: the effect, its interval and the decision it supports
quiz.explain: α is a decision rule fixed in advance, not a cliff; report the size and the uncertainty (→ 'Follow-ups an interviewer adds').

quiz.q: When is a one-sided test legitimate?
options: When the two-sided p is just above 0.05
Whenever n is small
When it was written down before the data and a result in the other direction would lead to the same action as 'no difference'
Always for rates
quiz.explain: Switching to one-sided after seeing the direction is the cheapest p-hacking there is (→ Day 3, 'One-sided or two-sided').

quiz.q: A fraud rule catches 90 % of frauds and flags 5 % of honest applicants. Fraud is 1 % of applications. What share of the flagged applications are fraud, in % (one decimal)?
quiz.explain: 0.9 × 0.01 / (0.9 × 0.01 + 0.05 × 0.99) = 15.4 %: about five flags in six are honest people. A good rule is still wrong most of the time when the thing it hunts is rare — the base-rate trap (→ Week 6 · Day 1, Bayes and the base-rate trap).

quiz.q: 400 loans, each with an FPD probability of 91 / 7 099. Which line gives P(8 or more FPDs)?
quiz.code: X = stats.binom(400, 91 / 7099)
options: X.sf(8)
X.sf(7)
X.cdf(8)
1 - X.pmf(8)
quiz.explain: sf(k) is P(X > k), so "k or more" is sf(k − 1). sf(8) is 9 or more (→ Week 6 · Day 1, Bernoulli and binomial).

quiz.q: Applicants' credit scores have a mean of 659.6 and a standard deviation of 59.5. What is the z-score of a score of 720 (two decimals)?
quiz.explain: z = (720 − 659.6) / 59.5 = 1.02: the score is about one standard deviation above the mean, so roughly 15 applicants in 100 score higher (→ Week 6 · Day 1, Normal — credit scores).

quiz.q: The average loan is 51.7 m soum and the median is 5.8 m soum. Which do you quote as the "typical" loan, and why?
options: The mean, because it uses every loan
The median, with a few percentiles: money is strongly skewed and a few huge loans pull the mean up
Either one, they differ only by rounding
The mode, because it is always the most useful
quiz.explain: The mean is almost nine times the median. For money, report the median and the percentiles (→ Week 6 · Day 1, Skew — when the mean and the median disagree).

quiz.q: The FPD rate is 91 / 7 099 = 1.28 %. What is the standard error of this rate, in percentage points (three decimals)?
quiz.explain: SE = √(p(1 − p) / n) = √(0.01282 × 0.98718 / 7 099) = 0.00134, about 0.13 points. This is the noise of the rate, not the spread of the loans (→ Week 6 · Day 2, Standard error).

quiz.q: A branch-month has 0 FPDs in 120 loans. What does the Wald interval give, and what do you report?
options: [0, 0], a zero-width interval. Report the Wilson interval instead: about 0 to 3.1 %
[0, 0]. The rate is certainly zero
A negative lower limit. Clip it to zero and report that
No interval can be computed for 0 events
quiz.explain: Wald's standard error is 0 when p = 0, so the interval collapses to a point. Wilson stays honest: with 0 events in 120 loans the rate could still be about 3 % (→ Week 6 · Day 2, The Wilson interval).

quiz.q: App FPD is 1.70 % (95 % CI 1.26–2.30 %) and branch FPD is 1.04 % (95 % CI 0.75–1.45 %). The intervals overlap. What can you say?
options: The channels do not differ
Overlap alone does not settle it: test the difference itself (here a two-proportion z-test gives p = 0.03)
The channel with the narrower interval is better
The intervals must be recomputed with Wald
quiz.explain: Two intervals can overlap and still be a real difference; the test of the difference is the right tool (→ Week 6 · Day 2, Mistakes people make; Week 6 · Day 3, Test for two proportions).

quiz.q: A test on 300 loans per group gives p = 0.20. Which statements are right?
options: There is not enough evidence of a difference. That is not proof of no difference
The two groups are the same
A larger sample could give a different answer
Before reading it as "no effect", check the power of the test
The probability that H₀ is true is 20 %
quiz.explain: p = 0.20 is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. With 300 loans per group and a rare outcome such as FPD the power is usually low. p is not the probability of H₀ (→ Week 6 · Day 3, Mistakes people make; Week 6 · Day 4, Power and sample size).

quiz.q: Does FPD30 depend on the risk grade (A, B, C, D)? Each loan has a grade and either an FPD or none. Which test fits?
options: Welch t-test on the four rates
Chi-square test of independence on the 4 × 2 table (grade × FPD)
Mann–Whitney U test
Paired t-test
quiz.explain: A yes/no outcome in three or more independent groups is a chi-square test of independence. If it is significant, compare pairs afterwards and correct for the number of pairs (→ Week 6 · Day 3, Chi-square test of independence; Week 6 · Day 4, reference card).

quiz.q: Kruskal–Wallis on the days late of the five products gives p < 0.001. What is the next step?
options: Report that all five products differ
Pairwise Mann–Whitney tests, corrected with Holm, to see which pairs differ
Repeat Kruskal–Wallis until p gets smaller
Switch to a t-test
quiz.explain: The omnibus test says only that some groups differ. The pairs come next, with a correction for the number of comparisons (→ Week 6 · Day 4, Kruskal–Wallis; Multiple comparisons).

quiz.q: You test 15 independent segments at α = 5 % and nothing is real. What is the chance of at least one false alarm, in % (one decimal)?
quiz.explain: 1 − 0.95¹⁵ = 53.7 %: more likely than not. Holm brings the family-wise error back to 5 % (→ Week 6 · Day 4, Multiple comparisons).

quiz.q: What does this return?
quiz.code: multipletests([0.004, 0.02, 0.03], method="holm")[1]
quiz.explain: Holm: the smallest p × 3 = 0.012, the next × 2 = 0.04, the last × 1 = 0.03. Adjusted p-values never go down along the sorted list, so the last one becomes 0.04. [0.012, 0.06, 0.09] is Bonferroni (→ Week 6 · Day 4, Multiple comparisons).

quiz.q: The chance that a test detects a real effect of the planned size is called its … (one word).
quiz.explain: Power = 1 − β. It is fixed before the data: it depends on α, the effect size, n and the noise (→ Week 6 · Day 4, Power and sample size).

quiz.q: A new product has 1 FPD in 40 loans. The old one has 6 in 300. If H₀ is true, the expected FPD count in the new product's cell is about 0.8. Which test do you report?
options: Chi-square without correction
Fisher's exact test, because the expected counts are far below 5
A two-proportion z-test
A paired t-test
quiz.explain: Chi-square and the z-test are approximations that need expected counts of about 5 or more. Fisher's test is exact at any n (→ Week 6 · Day 4, Chi-square or Fisher).

quiz.q: In the FPD frame, grade C has 44 FPDs in 2 034 loans and grade B has 30 in 3 084. How many more FPDs per 1 000 loans does grade C have (one decimal)?
quiz.explain: 44 / 2 034 = 2.16 % and 30 / 3 084 = 0.97 %. The gap of 1.19 points is 11.9 FPDs per 1 000 loans: an effect size in numbers a risk manager can use (→ Week 6 · Day 3, Effect size).

quiz.q: Two groups of applicants have different variances and different sizes. Which two-sample t-test do you use by default?
options: Student's t-test with a pooled variance
Welch's t-test (equal_var=False; in Excel =T.TEST(r1, r2, 2, 3))
A paired t-test
A z-test with σ = 1
quiz.explain: Welch needs no equal-variance assumption and loses almost nothing when the variances are equal (→ Week 6 · Day 3, Two-sample t-test).

quiz.q: Run it in the SQL playground. How many loans have an empty closed_at?
quiz.code: SELECT COUNT(*) - COUNT(closed_at) FROM loans;
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) counts the 7 828 rows and COUNT(closed_at) skips the empty values and counts 4 227, so 3 601 are empty. They are the open loans and the defaulted and written-off ones, plus 15 closed loans whose date was never filled in (→ Week 2 · Day 2, COUNT).

quiz.q: What does this query behave like?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN loans l ON l.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE l.status = 'active';
options: A LEFT JOIN: customers without a loan are counted too
An INNER JOIN: the WHERE on the right table throws the NULL rows away
An error: status is ambiguous
A CROSS JOIN
quiz.explain: A customer with no loan has NULL in l.status, the test = 'active' is not true for NULL, and the row is gone. The result, 3 352, is the same as with a plain JOIN. To keep the customers, move the condition into ON (→ Week 2 · Day 4, The LEFT JOIN that turns into an INNER JOIN).

quiz.q: Run it in the SQL playground. How many rows does it return?
quiz.code:
SELECT branch_id, COUNT(*) AS loans
FROM loans
GROUP BY branch_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 800;
quiz.explain: HAVING filters the groups after GROUP BY, so only the branches with more than 800 loans stay: Tashkent South, Tashkent North, Tashkent Central, Fergana Central and Samarkand Central. WHERE could not do this, because the count does not exist yet when WHERE runs (→ Week 2 · Day 2, WHERE vs HAVING).

quiz.q: Two branches: X approved 50 of 100 applications, Y approved 10 of 400. The total row of the Excel table needs one approval rate. What is it, in %?
quiz.explain: Sum the counts and divide once: 60 / 500 = 12 %. The simple average of the two rates, 26.25 %, ignores that Y is four times bigger (→ Week 4 · Day 1, Company corner).

quiz.q: The bucket table has the lower edges 0, 1, 31, 61 and 91 with the labels 0, 1-30, 31-60, 61-90 and 90+. Which label does this formula return for dpd = 61? Type the label.
quiz.code: =XLOOKUP(61, Lookup!$A$11:$A$15, Lookup!$B$11:$B$15, , -1)
quiz.explain: Match mode −1 takes the largest lower edge that is less than or equal to 61, which is 61 itself, so the label is 61-90. Day 60 would give 31-60 (→ Week 4 · Day 2, XLOOKUP for bands).

quiz.q: A column chart compares two branches with 120 bn and 130 bn outstanding. The value axis starts at 100 bn. How many times taller does the 130 bar LOOK than the 120 bar (one decimal)?
quiz.explain: The bars are drawn 30 and 20 units tall, so the eye reads "one and a half times" for an 8 % difference. Bars start at zero (→ Week 4 · Day 4, Chart trap: the truncated axis).

quiz.q: Each instalment's principal_due should show as a share of its loan's total principal_due on every row. Which call gives the loan total on every row?
options: inst.groupby('loan_id')['principal_due'].agg('sum')
inst.groupby('loan_id')['principal_due'].transform('sum')
inst['principal_due'].sum()
inst.sort_values('loan_id')['principal_due'].cumsum()
quiz.explain: transform returns one value per original row, like SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY loan_id) in SQL. agg returns one row per group (→ Week 5 · Day 3, transform).

quiz.q: 388 applications have no credit score. Which line counts them?
options: (apps['credit_score'] == np.nan).sum()
apps['credit_score'].isna().sum()
(apps['credit_score'] == '').sum()
apps['credit_score'].count()
quiz.explain: NaN is pandas' NULL. A comparison with == never finds it, because NaN is not equal to anything, not even to itself. isna() does. count() would give the 13 612 non-empty scores (→ Week 5 · Day 2, Missing values).

quiz.q: The loan with index label 5 has dpd = 0. What happens?
quiz.code:
late = loans[loans['dpd'] > 0]
late.loc[5]
options: It returns the first late loan
It raises KeyError: label 5 is not in late
It returns the sixth late loan
It returns NaN
quiz.explain: loc selects by label and iloc by position. After a filter the labels keep their old numbers, so late.iloc[0] is the first late loan and late.loc[5] fails (→ Week 5 · Day 2, loc and iloc).

w07d1.t: Week 7 · Day 1 — Designing an A/B test: before you touch the data

quiz.q: Why can 'September vs August' not tell Kamola whether the new screen works?
options: The months have different lengths
It can, if the change is large
September has fewer users
It changes two things at once — the screen and the calendar (season, marketing, policy, user mix)
quiz.explain: The app's approval rate moved four points between months with no change at all; a concurrent random control removes the calendar (→ section 1, 'Why September vs August is not an experiment').

quiz.q: For the offer screen you randomise by user. What breaks if you randomise and analyse sessions?
options: Conversion becomes higher
The hash cannot handle session ids
Nothing — sessions are more numerous
One person sees both screens, and her sessions are not independent, so the z-test's n is inflated
quiz.explain: The unit of analysis must equal the unit of randomisation (→ section 1, 'The unit of randomisation', P3).

quiz.q: The planned split is 50/50. What do you do with this result?
options: Treat it as a sign of a broken split: look for the bug by day, device and segment before trusting any result
Reweight B to 50 %
Read the result — 50.7 / 49.3 is close enough
Remove 400 users from A at random
quiz.explain: An SRM is not a bias to correct but a bug to find; check it overall and by slice (→ section 1, 'The sample-ratio mismatch (SRM) check', P7).

quiz.q: Why must the salt change between experiments?
options: SHA-256 runs out of values
The salt encrypts the user id
With the same salt the same users land in B every time — their history follows them and two tests are perfectly correlated
To make the split exactly 50/50
quiz.explain: The salt (the experiment name) makes assignments independent across experiments (→ section 1, 'Randomisation and assignment', P6).

quiz.q: You halve the MDE (from +0.9 to +0.45 points). The sample size per arm becomes about…
options: twice as large
half as large
the same
four times as large
quiz.explain: n grows with the inverse square of the effect: halving the effect quadruples the sample (→ section 1, 'Sample size and duration').

quiz.q: Which ways of looking keep an A/A test's false-positive rate near 5 %?
options: One look at the planned n on the planned end date
A live dashboard p-value used for the decision
Four weekly looks with Pocock's p < 0.0182 at each, decided before the start
O'Brien–Fleming boundaries decided before the start
Weekly looks, stopping at the first p < 0.05
quiz.explain: Daily looks gave 27 % false wins, weekly 12 %; sequential boundaries chosen in advance bring it back to about 5 % (→ section 1, 'Peeking').

quiz.q: B's true lift is +3.4 points on days 1–3 (novelty) and +0.9 afterwards, with equal traffic each day. What lift does a test that stops after 7 days report, in points?
quiz.explain: (3 × 3.4 + 4 × 0.9) / 7 = 1.97 — more than double the steady +0.9; run whole weeks and plan a daily lift chart (→ P9).

quiz.q: Company corner: why does the guardrail decision rest on the FPD difference's confidence interval rather than its p-value?
options: The CI is always narrower
With about 1 100 loans per arm the FPD test is weak; you compare the CI's upper bound with the break-even increase (+1.25 points)
Risk teams do not read p-values
p-values do not exist for FPD
quiz.explain: A guardrail needs a number — the break-even written in the pre-registration — and a weak test cannot clear it by 'not significant' (→ Company corner).

w07d2.t: Week 7 · Day 2 — Analysing the A/B test: the result, the traps, the decision

quiz.q: What do you check next?
quiz.code:
len(users), users["user_id"].nunique()
# (10000, 9900)
options: Which user ids have several rows, and whether those users were assigned to both variants
Drop the second row of each repeated user and move on
Reweight the arms
Nothing — 1 % is noise
quiz.explain: One row must be one user; a user who saw both screens belongs to neither arm, and events without a variant column would be counted in both (→ section 1, 'The data layout').

quiz.q: Which checks belong to step 1, before the primary result is read?
options: One row per user (rows vs unique ids)
The sample ratio overall and by the slices the software ships in (client × release week)
The daily lift chart for novelty
Holm-corrected segment results
Recompute every row's variant from the hash
