quiz.explain: Segments are step 4; a result read before the sanity checks is a number from a possibly broken machine (→ section 1, 'The order of an analysis').

quiz.q: The overall SRM p-value is 0.09. Is the split fine?
options: Not shown: a broken cell holding a few per cent of users is diluted overall; check by device × week and other release slices
Yes — p is above 0.05
No — p must be above 0.5
Only if every single day is fine too
quiz.explain: Slice by how the software ships; a daily check is too thin to see a small cell (→ section 1, 'Sanity check 1', P3).

quiz.q: You find a slice whose split is clearly broken. What do you do?
options: Remove its B users only
Keep it — the overall split is fine
Remove it from both arms, report the exclusion and its size — or re-run if it is large
Reweight it back to 50/50
quiz.explain: Within a broken cell the arms are not comparable; reweighting hides the bug instead of finding it (→ section 1, 'Sanity check 2', Mistakes).

quiz.q: How do you get the 95 % CI of the relative lift?
quiz.code:
lo, hi   = confint_proportions_2indep(kB, nB, kA, nA, method="newcomb")                  # difference B − A
rlo, rhi = confint_proportions_2indep(kB, nB, kA, nA, compare="ratio", method="log")    # ratio B / A
options: Divide lo and hi by A's rate
(hi − lo) / 2
A relative lift has no interval
rlo − 1 and rhi − 1, from the ratio's interval
quiz.explain: The relative interval comes from the ratio's CI (log method) minus 1, not from dividing the difference's limits by the control rate (→ section 1, 'The confidence interval for the lift', Mistakes).

quiz.q: A guardrail test on FPD gives p = 0.30, and its power was 25 %. What can you say?
options: Unresolved: compare the upper end of the difference's CI with the break-even; if it crosses, ship in stages with a hold-out
The guardrail passed
FPD got worse
Extend the test until p < 0.05
quiz.explain: 'Not significant' from an underpowered test means almost nothing (→ section 1, 'Guardrails', 'The result in one paragraph').

quiz.q: Seven pre-registered segments; the smallest raw p-value is 0.030. What is its Holm-adjusted p-value?
quiz.explain: Holm multiplies the smallest p by the number of tests: 0.030 × 7 = 0.21 — not significant; a segment difference also needs an interaction test (→ section 1, 'Segments').

quiz.q: Company corner: on the one-slide readout, which line comes right before the primary result?
options: What we learned
Sanity checks — what was removed and why, and the split after cleaning
The decision
Segments
quiz.explain: Hypothesis, design, sanity checks, primary, guardrails, segments, decision, learned — a slide that says what was removed survives the CFO (→ Company corner).

w07d3.t: Week 7 · Day 3 — Power BI I: get data, Power Query, the model

quiz.q: A table by product shows the same number in every row. What is the most likely cause?
options: The measure uses DIVIDE
Too many rows
A missing or inactive relationship — no filter can travel from products to that fact
A wrong data type
quiz.explain: Same value everywhere = missing relationship; a too-big total = wrong grain; (Blank) = keys that do not match (→ P6).

quiz.q: Power BI proposes a many-to-many relationship between products and a fact. What do you do?
options: Set cross-filter to Both
Accept it — it works
Find why the 'one' side is not unique (a duplicate key, a trailing space, a type mismatch) and fix the data
Delete the dimension
quiz.explain: The dimension side must be unique; never accept many-to-many to make the warning go away (→ section 1, 'Cardinality').

quiz.q: Why are bidirectional (Both) relationships dangerous?
options: They duplicate rows
They are slower but correct
They cannot be used with dates
A slicer then filters other dimensions and, through them, other facts — plausible-looking wrong numbers and ambiguous paths
quiz.explain: Single direction everywhere; when one measure needs the other direction, ask for it inside that measure (CROSSFILTER) (→ section 1, 'Cross-filter direction').

quiz.q: A card shows the Average of this column. What does it show?
quiz.code: is_par30 = IF ( v_loan_status[dpd] > 30, 1, 0 )      -- calculated column
options: NPL90
PAR30
Blank
The share of loans, by count and closed loans included, that are more than 30 days late — not a share of money
quiz.explain: PAR30 is a ratio of sums of money — a measure with DIVIDE(SUM, SUM); ratios are measures, never averages of row-level flags (→ section 1, 'Calculated column vs measure', P13).

quiz.q: v_payments_clean has 52 850 rows and loan_id is unique in v_loan_status. How many rows after this merge?
quiz.code:
Merge Queries: v_payments_clean <- v_loan_status on loan_id, Left Outer
Expand: product, branch_name only
quiz.explain: A merge is a lookup only when the right side is unique: rows stay 52 850; more rows would mean duplicate keys (→ section 1, 'Merge and Append', P4).

quiz.q: Which belong to the two-minute model check before any visual?
options: dim_date marked as the date table
Every relationship 1 : *, single direction, no unintended dashed line
Cross-filter set to Both so slicers reach everything
Row counts in Table view against the README
Load instead of Transform data, to save time
quiz.explain: Load skips the type check, and Both makes numbers silently wrong (→ section 1, 'Putting it together').

quiz.q: Which storage mode fits the Nur reports, and why?
options: Live connection to Excel
Composite — always best
Import — the data are copied into the .pbix, visuals are fast, all DAX works, and a refresh re-reads the views
DirectQuery — always live
quiz.explain: DirectQuery is for tables too big to copy or data that must be live (→ section 1, 'Import or DirectQuery').

quiz.q: Company corner: why not merge everything into one flat table for Power BI?
options: DAX needs at least two tables
Power BI cannot read flat tables
Flat tables refresh more slowly
Facts with different grains multiply each other's numbers: a loan's outstanding repeated on each payment sums to about 7 times the book
quiz.explain: Keep each fact at its grain and relate all facts to shared dimensions (→ Company corner).

w07d4.t: Week 7 · Day 4 — Power BI II: DAX and visuals that tell the story

quiz.q: In a matrix with one row per bucket, what does M90 show?
quiz.code: M90 = CALCULATE ( [Outstanding], v_loan_status[bucket] = "90+" )
options: Each bucket's own outstanding
90+'s outstanding in the 90+ row, blank elsewhere
90+'s outstanding in every row — the filter argument replaces the row's filter on bucket
An error
quiz.explain: A CALCULATE filter replaces existing filters on the same column; KEEPFILTERS intersects instead (→ section 1, 'CALCULATE', P4).

quiz.q: For loan 1, what does this calculated column hold?
quiz.code: own = CALCULATE ( SUM ( v_loan_status[outstanding] ) )      -- calculated column on v_loan_status
options: The whole book's outstanding
Blank
Loan 1's own outstanding — CALCULATE turns the row context into a filter (context transition)
An error: CALCULATE works only in measures
quiz.explain: Without CALCULATE, SUM in a column sees the whole table; with it, the row becomes a filter (→ section 1, 'Context transition', P5).

quiz.q: A branch slicer is set to Tashkent Central. Which denominator gives SME's share of the whole company's book?
options: CALCULATE ( [Outstanding], ALL ( products ) )
[Outstanding]
CALCULATE ( [Outstanding], ALLSELECTED ( products ) )
CALCULATE ( [Outstanding], ALL ( v_loan_status ) )
quiz.explain: ALL(products) removes only the product filter (share within the branch); ALL on the fact removes the filters arriving from its dimensions too (→ section 1, 'ALL and its relatives', P6).

quiz.q: You remove ALL from the RANKX branch rank. What happens?
options: The total row shows 1
Nothing changes
Every branch ranks 1 — each row's table holds only its own branch
Ranks reverse
quiz.explain: RANKX must iterate all branches; ALL removes the row's own branch filter (→ section 1, 'RANKX', P10).

quiz.q: Company corner: which measure goes on the Portfolio page's monthly trend line?
options: Outstanding Month-End — the last month's balance in the period, not a sum of balances
SUM of outstanding_month_end
Disbursed Amount
Outstanding (the as-of card measure)
quiz.explain: Outstanding is a balance dated by disbursement; balances are semi-additive, so the trend uses the month-end measure (→ section 1, 'Balances over time', Company corner).

quiz.q: What does time intelligence (TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR) need?
options: Dates stored as text
Each fact's own automatic date hierarchy
The fact related to dim_date
dim_date marked as the date table
dim_date contiguous — every day, no gaps
quiz.explain: Use dim_date everywhere; auto-date tables give a second calendar and a second answer (→ section 1, 'Time intelligence', P7).

quiz.q: Under the role 'Branch manager — Bukhara', the Branch Rank card shows 1. Bug or feature?
options: A bug in RANKX
The model is missing a relationship
The card is not synced
A feature: RLS removes other branches' rows before any measure runs, so ALL(branches) sees one branch; compute the rank upstream if she must see it
quiz.explain: RLS cannot be bypassed by DAX — that is the point (→ section 1, 'Row-level security', P14).

quiz.q: What does this measure show for September 2026, in % (two decimals)?
quiz.code:
Disbursed YoY % = DIVIDE ( [Disbursed Amount] - [Disbursed SPLY], [Disbursed SPLY] )
-- Sep 2026: Disbursed Amount 17 015 490 000 · Disbursed SPLY 14 644 540 000
quiz.explain: (17 015 490 000 − 14 644 540 000) / 14 644 540 000 = +16.19 %; DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error when last year is empty (→ section 1, 'Time intelligence').

w07d5.t: Week 7 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: A/B notebook + 3-page dashboard

quiz.q: B vs A gives p = 0.016. Which reading is right?
options: If the screens did not differ, a gap at least this large would appear in about 1.6 % of experiments of this size
B is 1.6 % better
1.6 % of users prefer A
There is a 98.4 % chance that B is better
quiz.explain: The p-value is computed assuming no difference; it is not the probability that B is better (→ A3 deductions, week 6 Day 3).

quiz.q: Some users were assigned to both arms. What do you do with them?
options: Keep their first assignment
Keep them — they are only 1 %
Remove only their second row
Remove every row of those users and report how many
quiz.explain: After the second assignment their outcome comes from a mix of A and B; they belong to neither arm (→ A1 deductions, Day 2 'The data layout').

quiz.q: Why a strict SRM threshold such as p < 0.001?
options: The regulator requires it
SRM is checked on many slices; a strict threshold keeps false alarms rare, and an alarm means a search for the bug
0.05 is for A/A tests only
The arms are large
quiz.explain: Many checks at 5 % would always raise something; the response to a real alarm is finding the cause, not reweighting (→ A1, Day 1 'SRM').

quiz.q: B converts better, yet z is negative. Why?
quiz.code:
z, p = proportions_ztest([conv_A, conv_B], [n_A, n_B])
# z = -2.41
options: A negative z means B is worse
The p-value must be halved
A is listed first, so z measures A − B; put B first or say which order you used
The test is broken
quiz.explain: An unexplained sign is a deduction; the worked example lists B first so that z > 0 means B is higher (→ A3 deductions).

quiz.q: Conversion goes from 8.0 % to 8.9 %. What is the relative lift, in %?
quiz.explain: 0.9 / 8.0 = 11.25 % relative; the absolute lift is +0.9 points — always say which (→ Warm-up 6).

quiz.q: Which are correct practices for the Part B dashboard?
options: Put the as-of Outstanding measure on the monthly trend line
Point the source at a parameter or a relative folder so the refresh works on Timur's PC
Sum Outstanding Month-End over the year
A pie chart of the five products
'Data as of 1 Oct 2026' and a definitions line on every page
Hide FPD vintages with fewer than 50 loans in scope
quiz.explain: The as-of Outstanding is dated by disbursement, month-end balances are not added, and a pie of five slices breaks the chart rules (→ Part B deductions).

quiz.q: What happens on a card when [Due] is 0 or blank, and what should you write instead?
quiz.code: Collection Rate = [Paid] / [Due]
options: It shows the company total
It shows Infinity or NaN instead of a blank; write DIVIDE ( [Paid], [Due] )
Power BI hides the card
It shows 0 % — fine
quiz.explain: DIVIDE returns blank (or a chosen value) when the denominator is 0 or blank — always DIVIDE for ratios (→ Day 4, 'The first measures').

quiz.q: One day of the test shows a lift of +5.2 points. Is that a novelty effect?
options: Yes, if p < 0.05 that day
No — novelty only exists in social apps
Yes — it is far above the average
Not by itself: single days swing by ±3 points; novelty is a pattern of the first days with a mechanism, excluded only as pre-registered
quiz.explain: Calling one high day 'novelty' is a listed deduction; exclusions must follow the pre-registered rule (→ A2 deductions, Day 2 'The daily lift').

w07d6.t: Week 7 · Day 6 — Section exam: A/B tests and Power BI (Week 7)

quiz.q: The offer-screen test needs 14 983 users per arm to detect a lift of +0.9 points. The team now wants to detect +0.3 points, a third of that. About how many times as many users per arm does it need?
quiz.explain: The sample grows with the inverse square of the effect. A third of the effect needs 3² = 9 times the users (→ Week 7 · Day 1, Sample size and duration).

quiz.q: The plan is 50/50. After a week A has 10 300 users and B has 9 700. What do you do?
options: Nothing: 51.5 % against 48.5 % is close enough to 50/50
Treat it as a sample ratio mismatch: look for the bug by day, device and release before you read any result
Reweight B up to 10 300 users
Remove 600 random users from A
quiz.explain: p ≈ 0.00002: chance cannot explain the gap. An SRM is a bug to find, not a bias to correct (→ Week 7 · Day 1, The sample-ratio mismatch (SRM) check).

quiz.q: Timur opens the running test every morning and wants to stop at the first day with p < 0.05. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing: stopping early saves money
Every look is another chance for noise to cross 0.05: with daily looks about one A/A test in four shows a false win (27 %), not one in twenty
The p-value is not computed before the end of the test
Daily looks need a larger α
quiz.explain: Fix the sample size and the end date in advance, or use boundaries made for repeated looks. Watch the guardrails and the SRM every day, but not the primary metric for a decision (→ Week 7 · Day 1, Peeking).

quiz.q: A new screen lifts conversion by +2.8 points on each of the first 4 days (novelty) and by +0.8 points on each of the next 10 days. The test stops after 14 days with equal traffic every day. What average lift does it report, in points (two decimals)?
quiz.explain: (4 × 2.8 + 10 × 0.8) / 14 = 1.37, well above the steady +0.8. A test that averages over the novelty days overstates the lift; plot the lift day by day (→ Week 7 · Day 1, Novelty and learning effects).

quiz.q: In the export, 180 users have rows in both A and B (about 1 % of the users). What do you do with them?
options: Keep their first assignment and drop the second
Remove every row of these users from both arms and report how many
Keep them: 1 % cannot matter
Assign them to the arm where they have more rows
quiz.explain: After the second assignment their outcome is a mix of A and B, so they belong to neither arm (→ Week 7 · Day 2, The data layout).

quiz.q: A test gives two groups exactly the same experience, to check the split, the logging and the analysis itself. It is written with two letters and a slash. What is it called? Type it like that.
quiz.explain: An A/A test checks the system, not the screen: the split should be 50/50, and the groups should differ "significantly" about 5 % of the time (→ Week 7 · Day 1, The A/A test — test the system, not the screen).

quiz.q: The primary result is B − A = +1.05 points, 95 % CI +0.14 to +1.98, p = 0.025. Which sentence is right?
options: B is better by exactly 1.05 points
Zero is outside the interval, so the lift is real. It could be as small as 0.14 or as large as 1.98 points, and the decision should use that range
There is a 97.5 % chance that B is better
The lift does not matter because the interval is wide
quiz.explain: The interval gives the size and its uncertainty. A p-value is not the probability that B is better (→ Week 7 · Day 2, The confidence interval for the lift).

quiz.q: The break-even FPD increase is +0.94 points. The guardrail test shows +0.5 points with a 95 % CI of −0.3 to +1.3, p = 0.22, and a power of 30 %. What do you say?
options: The guardrail is passed: p is above 0.05
It is unresolved: the upper end (+1.3) is above the break-even (+0.94). Ship in stages with a hold-out and read FPD later
FPD got worse, because +0.5 is positive
Extend the test until p < 0.05
quiz.explain: A weak test cannot clear a guardrail by being "not significant". Compare the upper end of the interval with the break-even written in the plan (→ Week 7 · Day 2, Guardrails; Week 7 · Day 1, Primary metric, secondary metrics, guardrails).

quiz.q: B converts better on weekdays (11 % against 10 %) and at weekends (5 % against 4 %), but worse in total (6.2 % against 8.8 %). What is going on, and what do you check first?
quiz.code:
A: users  converted    B: users  converted
weekday      800      80            200      22
weekend      200       8            800      40
options: B is better: the segments are the truth, ignore the total
B is worse: the total is the truth, ignore the segments
The arms got very different mixes of weekday and weekend traffic. A random split should not do that, so check the assignment (SRM and balance) before reading any result
Take the mean of 11 % and 5 % for B
quiz.explain: This is Simpson's paradox: B got mostly weekend users (800 of 1 000), where conversion is low. A balanced random split gives both arms the same mix, so this one is broken (→ Week 7 · Day 2, Simpson's paradox; Sanity check 3 — balance of the arms).

quiz.q: A matrix by product shows a (Blank) row with a few thousand soum of outstanding. What is the most likely cause?
options: A measure that uses DIVIDE
Fact rows whose product key has no match in the products table
The date table is not marked
Cross-filter set to Single
quiz.explain: (Blank) means keys that do not match. Fix the key or the dimension; do not hide the row with a filter (→ Week 7 · Day 3, Mistakes people make).

quiz.q: v_loan_status has 7 828 rows. You merge it with a products lookup on product_id (Left Outer, expand the name) and the result has 7 913 rows. What does that tell you?
options: 7 913 loans exist and the merge found 85 new ones
The lookup has duplicate product_id values: each duplicate repeats the loans of that key
A Left Outer merge always adds rows
The merge must be an Append
quiz.explain: A merge is a lookup only when the right side is unique. More rows than before means duplicate keys (→ Week 7 · Day 3, Merge and Append).

quiz.q: Which of these belong in a calculated column rather than in a measure?
options: A DPD bucket label to use in a slicer
PAR30 % for a card
An age band of the customer
Collection rate by month
An "is 90+" flag to filter rows
quiz.explain: Attributes you slice or filter by are columns, computed once per row at refresh. Ratios and anything aggregated are measures, evaluated in the filter context (→ Week 7 · Day 3, Calculated column vs measure; Week 7 · Day 4, Measure vs calculated column).

quiz.q: This measure sits in a table with one row per product, and a branch slicer is set to Bukhara Central. What does the row SME show?
quiz.code:
Product Share =
    DIVIDE ( [Outstanding],
             CALCULATE ( [Outstanding], ALL ( products ) ) )
options: SME's share of the whole company's book
SME's share of Bukhara Central's book, because ALL(products) removes only the product filter
100 % in every row
Blank in every row
quiz.explain: ALL(products) removes the filter that comes from the products table, so the denominator is the whole book of the selected branch. To ignore the branch slicer too, use ALL on the fact table (→ Week 7 · Day 4, ALL and its relatives).

quiz.q: TOTALYTD gives odd numbers for 2026. You find that the date table was built from the loan dates, so it has no row for a day with no disbursement. What is the fix?
options: Use the fact table's own date column
Build a date table with every day and no gaps, relate it to the fact and mark it as the date table
Turn on the automatic date hierarchies
Set the cross-filter to Both
quiz.explain: Time intelligence needs a contiguous date table, marked as such. Automatic hierarchies give a second calendar and a second answer (→ Week 7 · Day 4, Time intelligence).

quiz.q: What does this measure show for August 2026, in % (two decimals)?
quiz.code:
Disbursed YoY % =
    DIVIDE ( [Disbursed Amount] - [Disbursed SPLY], [Disbursed SPLY] )
-- Aug 2026: Disbursed Amount 22 290 210 000 · Disbursed SPLY 17 667 620 000
quiz.explain: (22 290 210 000 − 17 667 620 000) / 17 667 620 000 = +26.16 %. DIVIDE returns blank instead of an error when last year is empty (→ Week 7 · Day 4, Time intelligence).

quiz.q: How do you test a row-level security role in Power BI Desktop?
options: Open the report as yourself: if the numbers look right, the role works
Modeling → View as → the role, then compare the cards with the numbers you expect for that branch
Use ALL(branches) in a measure to see what is hidden
A role can only be tested in the Service, after publishing to everyone
quiz.explain: As yourself you see every row. View as applies the role's filter to every page and every measure. ALL(branches) cannot escape RLS, so a rank under RLS is always 1 (→ Week 7 · Day 4, Row-level security).

quiz.q: A test of B against A gives p = 0.04. Which reading is wrong?
options: If there were no difference, a gap this large or larger would appear in about 4 % of experiments of this size
There is a 96 % chance that B is better
It says nothing about how big the difference is
At an α of 5 % fixed in advance, we reject H₀
quiz.explain: The p-value is computed assuming H₀. It is not the probability that B is better, and it says nothing about the size (→ Week 6 · Day 3, The p-value — one right definition, three wrong ones).

quiz.q: A new partner has 2 FPDs in 80 loans. Which interval do you put on the dashboard?
options: Wilson, about 0.7 to 8.7 %
Wald, about −0.9 to 5.9 %
No interval: show the rate only
A bootstrap interval, because there are only 2 events
quiz.explain: Wald goes below zero and is too narrow near 0 %. Wilson stays inside 0–100 % and keeps its coverage. A bootstrap can only resample the 2 events it saw (→ Week 6 · Day 2, The Wilson interval).

quiz.q: Ten pre-registered segments, and the smallest raw p-value is 0.012. What is its Holm-adjusted p-value?
quiz.explain: Holm multiplies the smallest p-value by the number of tests: 0.012 × 10 = 0.12. It is not significant (→ Week 6 · Day 4, Multiple comparisons; Week 7 · Day 2, Segments).

quiz.q: The same 500 applications are scored by an old and a new scorecard, and each gives approve or reject. Which test compares the two approval rates?
options: Two-proportion z-test
McNemar's test on the applications where the two scorecards disagree
Welch t-test
Chi-square of independence on the two columns
quiz.explain: The outcome is yes/no measured twice on the same units, so it is paired. Only the applications where the scorecards disagree carry information (→ Week 6 · Day 4, reference card).

quiz.q: Run it in the SQL playground. How many different customers have a loan?
quiz.code: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM loans;
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) would give 7 828, the loans. COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) gives 4 335, the people. Report the one you mean (→ Week 2 · Day 2, COUNT).

quiz.q: A small book of four loans as of today. What is PAR30, in % (one decimal)?
quiz.code:
loan | dpd | outstanding
A    |   0 | 400
B    |  20 | 100
C    |  75 |  60
D    | 200 |  40
quiz.explain: PAR30 = outstanding of loans with DPD > 30 ÷ total outstanding = (60 + 40) / 600 = 16.7 %. NPL90 would be 40 / 600 = 6.7 % (→ Week 3 · Day 4, Company corner).

quiz.q: XLOOKUP returns #N/A for "Auto loan", a product that is clearly in the Lookup table. What is the likely cause?
quiz.code:
A2 shows: Auto loan
=LEN(A2)   →   10
options: A trailing space in the key: "Auto loan" has 9 characters, so TRIM it
XLOOKUP is case-sensitive
The return column number is wrong
The match mode should be 1
quiz.explain: #N/A means nothing matched. Check spaces with LEN and numbers stored as text with ISNUMBER (→ Week 4 · Day 5, Follow-ups a panel asks).

quiz.q: You want to keep the earliest payment_id among exact duplicates of (installment_id, paid_at, amount). Which line does it?
options: pay.drop_duplicates(['installment_id', 'paid_at', 'amount'])
pay.sort_values('payment_id').drop_duplicates(['installment_id', 'paid_at', 'amount'])
pay.drop_duplicates()
pay.duplicated().sum()
quiz.explain: drop_duplicates keeps the first row it meets, so sort first. Without subset it compares every column and finds nothing, because payment_id differs (→ Week 5 · Day 3, Duplicates — find, look, then drop).

quiz.q: Both lines return the same count for ch = "app". Which one belongs in a report that other people will run?
quiz.code:
a = pd.read_sql(f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM applications WHERE channel = '{ch}'", con)
b = pd.read_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM applications WHERE channel = ?", con, params=(ch,))
options: The first, because an f-string is easy to read
The second: params= passes the value safely, while an f-string breaks on a quote and invites injection
Neither: use string concatenation
Both are the same
quiz.explain: Values go in params=, never into the SQL text (→ Week 5 · Day 4, read_sql).

w08d1.t: Week 8 · Day 1 — Product analytics I: metrics that matter, funnels and retention

quiz.q: What makes a metric tree multiply back to the total exactly?
options: Each factor uses the same month's calendar data
Approval must exclude cancelled applications
Every factor is a percentage
Each factor's denominator is the previous factor's numerator — so the tree's approval rate is approved ÷ all applications
quiz.explain: The product telescopes only when the chain is consistent; the risk report's approved ÷ decided is fine, just not in the tree (→ section 1, 'A metric tree').

quiz.q: Active customers 2 846; application rate 22.80 %; approval (tree) 60.40 %; take-up 92.60 %. About how many loans did August's applications produce?
quiz.explain: 2 846 × 0.2280 × 0.6040 × 0.9260 ≈ 363 — the tree multiplies back to the 363 loans and 23.3 bn of the worked example (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Why is this not the funnel's 'reached' count?
options: GROUP BY must come before FROM
COUNT(*) skips NULLs
It is the correct funnel
It counts events, not sessions; reached = has the event, once per session — MAX(CASE …) per application_id, then SUM
quiz.explain: In this data each step happens at most once per session, but the definition must not depend on that luck (→ section 1, 'The lending funnel', ⚠️).

quiz.q: A dashboard says '64 % of applicants drop before opening the app'. What is the first question?
options: Who is in the denominator — app_events exists only for applications made in the app
Whether the app crashed
What the drop was last month
Which app version they used
quiz.explain: Branch and partner customers never had an app session to lose; an app funnel must say 'app applications only' (→ P4).

quiz.q: device and app_version are logged per event and change inside a session. How do you group the funnel by device?
options: By the most common device in the table
You cannot group by device
By each event's own device
By session, taking the device of the session's app_open
quiz.explain: Grouping events by their own device counts each step on a different population — the 'iOS advantage' was an artefact (→ section 1, 'Leaky steps', check 3, P5).

quiz.q: Which are leading metrics?
options: FPD30 at 60 days
Applications this week
NPL90 after a year
Write-offs
1–30 DPD entries
quiz.explain: Leading metrics move before the result; NPL90 and write-offs confirm it later (→ section 1, 'A metric tree').

quiz.q: What is wrong, and what is the fix?
quiz.code:
-- repeat borrowing, first-loan cohort 2026-06
-- m3 = 37.4 % · m6 = 37.4 % · m12 = 37.4 %
options: Nothing — these customers repeat early
The 6- and 12-month windows have not ended for this cohort; blank a cell unless every first loan of the cohort is at least N months old
Use COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
Start the cohort at the application date
quiz.explain: An unobservable cell is 'not measured', not 'did not repeat' — the same rule as week 3's vintage blanks (→ section 1, 'The retention table and the retention curve', P8).

quiz.q: Company corner: on the net-income tree, which branch does Sevara's cure rate belong to?
options: Operating expenses
Cost of risk → LGD
Interest income → yield
Disbursements → take-up
quiz.explain: Cure rate, recoveries and restructuring drive LGD, a child of cost of risk (→ Company corner).

w08d2.t: Week 8 · Day 2 — Product analytics II and the company day: unit economics, storytelling, the job

quiz.q: Finance asks where the next billion of funding earns most. Which number do you show?
options: The number of loans
Net contribution per 1 000 soum lent
Interest income per loan
Net contribution per loan
quiz.explain: Per loan says which product is worth a salesperson's afternoon; per soum says where money earns most — they can rank products differently (→ section 1, 'Contribution margin per loan').

quiz.q: Which line misstates loan 1's cost of funds, and how?
quiz.code:
I   = inst["interest_due"].sum()           # line 1: 10 650 293
cof = 31_150_000 * 0.18 / 12 * 24            # line 2
net = (1 - PD) * I - cof - el - acq - serv   # line 3
options: line 1 — interest must be (1 − PD) × I
No line — it is correct
line 3 — EL should be added, not subtracted
line 2 — it charges funding on the original principal for 24 months; it should be on the falling balance before each instalment (6.39 m, not 11.21 m)
quiz.explain: Both the borrower's interest and Nur's funding cost run on the falling annuity balance (→ section 1, 'Cost of funds', section 2).

quiz.q: Loan 1 earns a net contribution of 2 392 852 soum on a principal of 31 150 000. What is that per 1 000 soum lent (one decimal)?
This crude PD is computed on all loans of each product. For which products does it understate risk most?
quiz.code: PD = (ls["dpd"] > 90).groupby(ls["code"]).mean()     # share of loans now 90+, all ages
options: Short products like Micro
None — it is unbiased
Long, young products like SME — most of their loans have not had time to default
BNPL, because it charges 0 %
quiz.explain: Recompute PD on matured loans (last instalment due by the as-of): SME's rises from 3.7 % to about 9 % and its margin per soum falls by two thirds (→ P8).

quiz.q: LTV/CAC for app customers is about 48 on average, but most of the LTV comes from a few SME and Auto loans. How do you report it?
options: Drop the SME loans as outliers
Separately: the typical (Micro-only) LTV/CAC is about 1.6; the few who later take branch loans are very valuable
Report the median CAC
'Every app customer is worth 48 times their CAC'
quiz.explain: An average lifted by a few huge cross-sold loans is not what a typical customer delivers (→ P10).

quiz.q: Which is a so-what title?
options: Product analysis, Q3
SME and Auto earn 60–73 soum per 1 000 lent; BNPL loses 108
Unit economics by product
Methodology and data sources
quiz.explain: A title is a sentence with a number and a comparison that says what to conclude (→ section 1, 'Telling it — the answer first').

quiz.q: Which statements about IFRS 9 and cost of risk are true?
options: Cost of risk is mostly the change in provisions plus write-offs minus recoveries
Defaulted loans (usually 90+ DPD) carry lifetime loss on a defaulted exposure
Healthy loans carry 12 months of expected loss
Loans whose risk grew significantly (often 30+ DPD) carry lifetime expected loss
A provision is booked only once a loss has happened
quiz.explain: IFRS 9 provisions for the loss we expect, so a rise in 1–30 DPD costs money this month (→ section 4, 'Regulators and reporting').

quiz.q: Company corner: FPD30 or PAR30 — which moves first when new loans get worse?
options: PAR30 — it covers the whole book
Neither — only NPL moves
They move together
FPD30 — a property of a cohort of new loans, known two months after disbursement; PAR30 moves months later, diluted by the old book
quiz.explain: FPD is the leading signal; PAR30 is the state of the whole book today (→ Company corner, question 2).

w08d3.t: Week 8 · Day 3 — Capstone I: the brief and the analysis

quiz.q: An issue tree should be MECE: mutually exclusive and collectively … (one word)
quiz.explain: No overlaps, no gaps — each leaf a question one table can answer (→ section 6).

quiz.q: What makes a branch hypothesis useful?
options: It is vague enough to always be true
It comes with a test that could break it — 'SME grows fastest and earns most, unless its matured default rate is much higher'
It has no number
It matches what the board already believes
quiz.explain: A hypothesis you cannot break is an opinion (→ section 6).

quiz.q: Your app FPD30 is 1.9 %; the sanity table says 1.70 %. What do you check first?
options: Clean vs raw payments, the maturity rule (first instalment due on or before 2026-09-01) and the denominator
Drop the app from the analysis
Switch to a one-sided test
Nothing — update the sanity table
quiz.explain: If a sanity number differs, find out why before building on it — usually raw payments, BETWEEN on a datetime, a status list or immature loans (→ section 7).

quiz.q: Which handlings of the known data problems are right?
options: Use closed_at to decide whether a loan is live
Build the app funnel on all applications
FPD only for first instalments due on or before 2026-09-01
Sum money from v_payments_clean
Leave unobservable vintage cells blank
quiz.explain: closed_at is empty for some closed loans (use status and the schedule), and app_events exist only for app applications (→ section 7, 'Known problems').

quiz.q: applied_at holds a date and a time. What does this filter lose?
quiz.code: WHERE applied_at BETWEEN '2026-09-01' AND '2026-09-30'
options: Nothing
Every application after midnight on 30 September
Only applications with NULL dates
Applications on 1 September
quiz.explain: '2026-09-30' means 00:00 on the 30th; use >= '2026-09-01' AND < '2026-10-01' — the half-open rule (→ section 7, sanity-number tips).

quiz.q: Why COUNT(t.loan_id) for 'contacted'?
options: It counts distinct loans
After a LEFT JOIN, t.loan_id is NULL for loans with no action, and COUNT(column) skips NULLs — so only contacted loans are counted
It equals COUNT(*)
COUNT(*) would fail
quiz.explain: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(column) counts non-null values — the week-2 NULL rule doing the work (→ section 8).

quiz.q: SME disbursement grew strongly in amount. What must sit next to it?
options: The median principal only
Nothing — amount is what the board wants
The approval rate
The count of loans: amount growth can be a few very large loans, not more borrowing
quiz.explain: Count and amount, always both (→ section 9, 'Common pitfalls').

quiz.q: How do you judge collections efficiency?
options: By the outcomes collectors record ('paid')
By the share of SMS
By the number of calls
By actual payments after the action, from the payments table
quiz.explain: Recorded outcomes are a collector's note, not money (→ section 9, 'Common pitfalls').

w08d4.t: Week 8 · Day 4 — Capstone II: dashboard and story

quiz.q: What is the governing thought?
options: The title of the deck
The first finding in the notebook
A list of the five questions
One sentence that answers the chairman's question: grow X and Y, slow Z until …, change A and B — worth about N
quiz.explain: If you cannot write it, go back to the issue tree, not to PowerPoint (→ section 2).

quiz.q: Read as a ghost deck, which titles must be rewritten?
quiz.code:
1. Context
2. Growth by region
3. The fastest-growing region also carries the highest PAR30
4. Unit economics
quiz.explain: Titles 1, 2 and 4 are topics; only 3 is a sentence with a comparison and a 'so what' (→ section 3).

quiz.q: You want to show growth vs PAR30 for each region. Which chart?
options: A pie per region
A dual-axis line chart
A gauge
A scatter with labelled points (or two aligned bar columns)
quiz.explain: Two measures per category: scatter or aligned bars; dual axes invent crossings (→ section 4).

quiz.q: How do you draw vintage curves?
options: One bar per cohort
Lines that continue to the last month for every cohort
Lines by cohort vs MOB that stop where the months are not yet observable (or a heat-mapped table with blanks)
A pie per cohort
quiz.explain: Unobservable months are blank, never 0 or a continued line (→ section 4, Day 3 correctness traps).

quiz.q: fct_first_instalment has one row per loan in FPD scope. With a product slicer on MICRO, what does this card show?
quiz.code: FPD30 % = DIVIDE ( SUM ( fct_first_instalment[fpd30] ), COUNTROWS ( fct_first_instalment ) )
options: MICRO's FPD30 among its loans in scope
FPD30 of all MICRO loans, immature ones included
MICRO's share of all FPDs
Blank — slicers cannot reach this table
quiz.explain: SUM of the 0/1 flag ÷ rows is the rate in the filter context; the table already applies the maturity rule (→ section 5, Day 3 sanity numbers).

quiz.q: Nilufar: 'Your PD is crude. Why should I believe your margins?' What is the best answer?
options: Agree first, then show how it moves the answer — the matured-PD sensitivity
Change the subject to growth
Defend the crude PD
Say risk models are her job
quiz.explain: Agree, then quantify: a recommendation must survive its assumptions (→ section 8).

quiz.q: Sevara's team contacts mostly loans that are 90+ now. Which caveat do you raise before she does?
options: The bucket is today's, not the bucket at the time of the action — a loan called at 20 DPD may be 120 DPD now
September is a short month
SMS are cheaper than calls
The data are synthetic
quiz.explain: Say what the data show and what you do not know; prepare the version with DPD at the action date if you can (→ section 8).

quiz.q: A board member asks for a cut you do not have. What do you say?
options: Say it does not matter
Change the subject
'I don't have that cut here; I will check and send it today' — and write it down
Guess the likely cause
quiz.explain: Never guess a cause in front of risk; a number or 'I will check' (→ section 8, Day 5 'The ten minutes').

w08d5.t: Week 8 · Day 5 — Presentation day, the mock interview, and what next

quiz.q: How do you open the ten-minute presentation?
options: 'Today I will talk about…'
With the method
With the answer: the governing thought and three bullets
With the data sources
quiz.explain: The answer comes in the first minute; the rest is evidence (→ Part A, 'The ten minutes').

quiz.q: A board member disagrees with one of your numbers. What do you do?
options: Thank them, restate their point, give your number and its definition, and offer the check that would settle it
Argue until they accept it
Drop the slide
Change the number
quiz.explain: Never argue about a number whose definition you have not agreed (→ Part A, 'The ten minutes').

quiz.q: Two officers in one branch tie for the most approvals. What does this return for that branch?
quiz.code:
r AS (SELECT o.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY branch_id ORDER BY approved DESC) AS rn FROM o)
SELECT * FROM r WHERE rn = 1;
options: Both officers
An error
Neither
One of them, chosen silently — RANK() keeps the tie
quiz.explain: ROW_NUMBER always numbers 1, 2, …; RANK gives tied rows the same rank (→ B2, T3).

quiz.q: This is meant to find each customer's first loan, for customers whose first loan was in 2025. What goes wrong?
quiz.code:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT customer_id, disbursed_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY disbursed_at, loan_id) AS n
  FROM loans
  WHERE disbursed_at >= '2025-01-01' AND disbursed_at < '2026-01-01')
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE n = 1;
options: loan_id in ORDER BY breaks the ranking
The date filter runs before ROW_NUMBER, so a customer's first 2025 loan looks like a first loan even if they borrowed in 2024
Nothing
ROW_NUMBER needs GROUP BY
quiz.explain: Find the first loan on all loans, then filter the cohort (→ B2, T4).

quiz.q: Case: 'FPD in the app doubled last month.' What is your first step?
options: Re-train the scorecard
Check that it is real and how big: the definition, which month, and how many loans and defaults — 1 → 2 defaults on ~120 loans is 'doubled'
Recommend pausing the app
Look for a fraud ring
quiz.explain: Most candidates skip reality and size; only then locate it, separate mix from rate, and recommend (→ B3).

quiz.q: STAR stands for Situation, Task, Action and … (one word)
quiz.explain: Tell the result with a number, not the tools you used (→ B1).

quiz.q: Which are good first questions to ask the interviewer?
options: What is the salary, and how many holidays are there?
What would a successful first three months look like in this role?
What does the company do?
What is the biggest data-quality problem the team lives with today?
Which definition of approval rate or NPL do you use in the board pack?
quiz.explain: Ask about the work, the data and the team; perks come later with HR, and you should already know what the company does (→ B5).

quiz.q: What is the goal of your first 30 days in an analyst job?
options: Rebuild the warehouse
Learn the business and the data: meet the internal clients, write a glossary of their definitions, rebuild one recurring report and reconcile it to the soum
Automate every manual step
Deliver a big analysis that changes a decision
quiz.explain: Learn, then deliver (31–60), then improve (61–90) (→ Part C, the 30/60/90-day plan).

w08d6.t: Week 8 · Day 6 — Section exam: Product analytics and the job (Week 8)

quiz.q: A small example of a metric tree: 3 100 active customers; application rate 20 %; approval (tree definition, approved ÷ all applications) 55 %; take-up 90 %. About how many loans does the month produce?
quiz.explain: 3 100 × 0.20 × 0.55 × 0.90 = 306.9 ≈ 307. The factors multiply back to the total only when each denominator is the previous numerator (→ Week 8 · Day 1, A metric tree).

quiz.q: Run it in the SQL playground. How many app applications have the event start_application but never the event submit_application?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM app_events s
WHERE s.event_name = 'start_application'
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM app_events t
                  WHERE t.application_id = s.application_id
                    AND t.event_name = 'submit_application');
quiz.explain: 4 003 applications started the form and 3 451 submitted it, so 552 stopped in between: 13.8 % of those who started (→ Week 8 · Day 1, The lending funnel; Leaky steps).

quiz.q: A slide says: "Only 20.8 % of applications end in a signed contract." It divides the 2 915 signed contracts by all 14 000 applications. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: 20.8 % is the funnel
app_events exist only for the 5 006 applications made in the app. The app funnel is read on those: 2 915 of 5 006 = 58.2 %
Signed contracts should be divided by approved applications
The numerator should be disbursed loans only
quiz.explain: Branch and partner customers have no app events at all, so they cannot drop out of an app funnel. Say "app applications only" and divide by app_open (→ Week 8 · Day 1, The lending funnel).

quiz.q: It is 1 October 2026. The retention table has a cohort row for January 2026. What goes in its 12-month cell?
options: The share measured so far, as if 12 months had passed
Nothing: the cell stays blank, because 12 months have not passed for any customer of the cohort
The 6-month value
quiz.explain: An unobservable cell is "not measured", not "did not return". A cell is shown only when every first loan of the cohort is at least N months old (→ Week 8 · Day 1, The retention table and the retention curve).

quiz.q: Which metric warns first that a new channel brings weaker borrowers?
options: NPL90 a year later
FPD30 of the channel's new loans, known about two months after disbursement
Write-offs
PAR30 of the whole book
quiz.explain: FPD30 is a property of a cohort of new loans and is a leading signal. PAR30 moves months later, diluted by the old book (→ Week 8 · Day 2, Company corner; Week 8 · Day 1, A metric tree).

quiz.q: Why is DAU/MAU a poor headline metric for a lender?
options: It cannot be computed from app_events
People open a lender's app when they need money, a few times a year, so low stickiness is normal and says little about the business. A money-linked metric, such as repeat borrowing, fits better
MAU is always smaller than DAU
It counts customers twice
quiz.explain: Stickiness of 3–4 % is normal for a lender. The North Star should be linked to money, such as repeat borrowing or disbursed loans (→ Week 8 · Day 1, Active users — DAU, MAU and what "active" means here).

quiz.q: An average Consumer loan has PD = 77 of 2 418 loans now 90+ days past due. Take LGD = 70 % (harsher than the course's 60 %) and EAD = 21 630 783 soum. What is the expected loss, in soum, to the nearest 1 000?
quiz.explain: EL = PD × LGD × EAD = 0.03184 × 0.70 × 21 630 783 ≈ 482 000 soum per loan. At 60 % it is 413 000: the LGD guess moves the cost of risk by a sixth (→ Week 8 · Day 2, Cost of risk).

quiz.q: Finance asks where the next billion of funding earns most. At Nur, SME leads on contribution per loan (18.6 m soum) and Auto leads per 1 000 soum lent (72.9). Which number do you show?
options: SME's 18.6 m per loan
Auto's 72.9 per 1 000 soum lent: per soum answers where money earns most
The number of loans
Interest income
quiz.explain: Per loan says which sale is worth a salesperson's afternoon. Per soum says where the next billion earns most. Say which question you answer before you rank anything (→ Week 8 · Day 2, Contribution margin per loan).

quiz.q: A toy loan: interest I = 4 000 000, cost of funds 2 200 000, acquisition plus servicing 400 000, LGD × EAD = 9 000 000. Break-even PD* = (I − CoF − acq − serv) ÷ (I + LGD × EAD). What is it, in % (one decimal)?
quiz.explain: (4 000 000 − 2 200 000 − 400 000) ÷ (4 000 000 + 9 000 000) = 1 400 000 ÷ 13 000 000 = 10.8 %. Report the break-even next to any guessed input (→ Week 8 · Day 2, Break-even).

quiz.q: CAC is 150 000 soum. A loan's contribution before acquisition is 720 000 soum over a 12-month term. What is the payback, in months (one decimal)?
quiz.explain: Payback = CAC ÷ (contribution before acquisition ÷ term) = 150 000 ÷ 60 000 = 2.5 months. Use the contribution before acquisition, or the CAC is paid twice (→ Week 8 · Day 2, CAC and payback).

quiz.q: SME is 781 of the 7 828 loans and 241.1 bn of the 404.8 bn lent. Which title for the SME slide follows the so-what rule?
options: SME: loan statistics
SME is 10 % of our loans but 60 % of the money lent
Product mix, 2024–2026
Appendix: SME
quiz.explain: A title is a sentence with a number and a comparison: 781 / 7 828 = 10.0 % of the loans and 241.1 / 404.8 = 59.6 % of the money (→ Week 8 · Day 2, Telling it — the answer first; Week 8 · Day 4, The ghost deck).

quiz.q: Which statements about IFRS 9 provisions are true, as the course teaches them?
options: A healthy loan (stage 1) carries 12 months of expected loss
More than 30 days past due puts a loan in stage 2, with lifetime expected loss
Stage 3 starts after 90 days past due
A provision is booked only once a loss has happened
A loan at 45 days past due needs no provision yet
quiz.explain: IFRS 9 provides for the loss we expect, not only the loss that has happened. So a rise in early delinquency moves loans to stage 2 and costs money in the P&L now (→ Week 8 · Day 2, Going further — IFRS 9 provisions).

quiz.q: An FPD30 rate is computed on all 7 828 loans, including the ones disbursed last week. What is wrong?
options: Nothing
Young loans have not had their 30 days, so they count as "not FPD" and make the rate look too good. Keep the loans whose first instalment fell due at least 30 days before the as-of date
FPD needs 90 days
FPD30 must leave out the app loans
quiz.explain: Every loan in the base must have had the chance to fail. The sanity table's 7 099 loans follow this rule (→ Week 2 · Day 4, Company corner; Week 8 · Day 3, Sanity numbers).

quiz.q: The approval rate dropped 5 points last week, on about 150 decisions. What do you check first?
options: Re-train the scorecard
Whether it is real: the same definition, a complete week (pending applications count as not approved) and the interval, because 5 points can be noise on 150 decisions
Which collector is to blame
Lower the cut-off
quiz.explain: Most candidates skip "is it real and how big". Then comes mix against rate, the funnel step and the money (→ Week 8 · Day 5, The case method).

quiz.q: Product says the app's conversion is 58 %. Risk says its approval rate is 68 %. Both numbers are right. How can that be?
options: One of them has a bug
Different denominators: 58 % is approved ÷ app sessions, 68 % is approved ÷ decided applications. Write the definition under each number
They are measured in different years
Cancelled applications are rounded
quiz.explain: 2 915 approved ÷ 5 006 app sessions = 58.2 %; 2 915 ÷ 4 274 decided = 68.2 %. Do not assume either side is wrong: reconcile the definitions and tell the owner (→ Week 1 · Day 2, Company corner; interview bank E1).

quiz.q: Your unit economics rest on an assumed funding cost and an assumed LGD. What do you add to the recommendation?
options: Nothing: assumptions are facts once they are written down
A sensitivity: show how the answer moves if funding or LGD changes, with the break-even, so the recommendation survives its assumptions
Delete the assumptions slide
Use the best case only
quiz.explain: Your cost figures are assumptions, not facts. One sensitivity makes the recommendation credible (→ Week 8 · Day 3, Common pitfalls; Week 8 · Day 4, the questions each board member will ask).

quiz.q: The standard error of a rate is 0.8 points with 1 000 loans. How many loans give a standard error of 0.4 points?
quiz.explain: SE shrinks like 1 / √n. To halve it you need four times the sample: 4 000 loans (→ Week 6 · Day 2, Standard error).

quiz.q: A test on 40 000 payments gives p = 10⁻⁹ for a gap of 0.04 points in the late-payment rate. What do you report?
options: Highly significant, so it is important
Significant but tiny: report the effect size with its interval and what it is worth in money, and compare it with a break-even
Nothing: a p-value that small cannot be real
Drop rows until p is above 0.05
quiz.explain: p depends on n: with enough rows any gap is significant. Importance is the size of the effect in business units (→ Week 6 · Day 3, Effect size; interview bank D3).

quiz.q: You randomise customers to A or B but analyse applications, and a customer can have several. What breaks?
options: Nothing
The applications of one customer are not independent, so the z-test overstates the n and the p-value is too small
Conversion always falls
The hash stops working
quiz.explain: The unit of analysis must equal the unit of randomisation: analyse customers, or use a method that handles clusters (→ Week 7 · Day 1, The unit of randomisation).

quiz.q: Writing down the metric, the sample size, the end date and the stopping rule before a test starts is called … (one word, with a hyphen).
quiz.explain: A pre-registered plan means nobody can choose the metric, the segment or the stopping day after seeing the data. It turns a reading you can bend into a reading you can trust (→ Week 7 · Day 1, Pre-registration — the one-page test plan).

quiz.q: In a matrix with one row per product, what does the row SME show?
quiz.code:
Outstanding Auto =
    CALCULATE ( [Outstanding], products[code] = "AUTO" )
options: SME's outstanding in the SME row and blank elsewhere
Auto's outstanding in every row, because the filter argument replaces the row's own filter on products[code]
Blank in every row except Auto
An error
quiz.explain: A CALCULATE filter replaces the existing filters on the same column; KEEPFILTERS would intersect them instead (→ Week 7 · Day 4, CALCULATE).

quiz.q: What does this query return? Applications with status 'approved' or 'approved_not_disbursed' are 8 595 of the 14 000.
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(CASE WHEN status LIKE 'approved%' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
FROM applications;
quiz.explain: COUNT counts the non-NULL values, and ELSE 0 is not NULL, so every row is counted. Leave out the ELSE, or use SUM(CASE … THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) (→ Week 2 · Day 4, CASE inside SUM and COUNT).

quiz.q: Run it in the SQL playground. SUM(l.principal) after this join is how many times the true total of lent principal, to one decimal? (Compare it with SELECT SUM(principal) FROM loans.)
quiz.explain: The join returns 92 193 rows, one per instalment, and each loan's principal is counted once per instalment: 9 981 530 850 000 against 404 783 280 000, which is 24.7 times. Check COUNT(*) against COUNT(DISTINCT l.loan_id) before you sum (→ Week 2 · Day 1, Many-to-one and one-to-many; Week 2 · Day 2, Aggregating over a join).

quiz.q: A report wraps every lookup in IFERROR(…, 0) and its totals always look complete. What is the risk, and what do you add?
options: None: IFERROR makes formulas robust
Missing keys turn silently into zeros and the total is wrong with no warning. Use IFERROR only when a miss is expected, and add a check cell that counts the misses
IFERROR slows the sheet
IFERROR switches the lookup to approximate match
quiz.explain: A miss should be visible, counted and then handled (→ Week 4 · Day 2, IFERROR).

quiz.q: A customer earns exactly 10 000 000 soum. Which income band does this put the customer in?
quiz.code: pd.cut(lc["monthly_income"], [0, 5e6, 10e6, 20e6, np.inf], right=False)
options: NaN
quiz.explain: right=False makes each interval closed on the left, so 10 000 000 sits in [10m, 20m). It matches SQL's WHEN monthly_income < 10000000 (→ Week 5 · Day 5, S10).

w09d1.t: Week 9 · Day 1 — Correlation and linear regression: what moves the monthly payment?

quiz.q: What does Pearson's r measure?
options: How steep the line is
How closely the dots lie to a straight line, and its direction
Whether x causes y
The share of y explained, in %
quiz.explain: r is direction and closeness to a line, from −1 to +1; steepness is the slope, and the share explained is R² (→ section 1, 'Pearson's correlation r').

quiz.q: Across all loans r(term, payment) = +0.335; inside every product it is negative. Why?
options: The book-wide number is wrong
The product is a confounder: Auto and SME loans are both long and big, so mixing products makes 'longer' look like 'bigger payment'
Small groups always give negative r
Payments are rounded
quiz.explain: Simpson's paradox: a third variable can flip a correlation between the pooled data and every group (→ section 1, 'Correlation is not causation').

quiz.q: A line has r = 0.6. What R², in %?
quiz.explain: R² = r² = 0.36 → 36 % (→ section 1, 'R²').

quiz.q: Principal has skewness 2.9. Term against principal: Pearson 0.581, Spearman 0.713. Which statement is right?
options: Spearman is wrong because it ignores the values
The ranks show a cleaner 'longer goes with bigger' than the skewed values; report Spearman for money columns
Pearson is always better
The two must be equal
quiz.explain: Spearman uses ranks, so a handful of huge loans cannot drag it; it measures a monotonic pattern (→ section 1, 'Spearman').

quiz.q: What is wrong with this cell, meant to explain the payment by the principal?
quiz.code: b, a = np.polyfit(auto["pay_k"], auto["pm"], 1)
options: Nothing
x and y are swapped: polyfit takes x first, so this regresses the principal on the payment
The degree should be 2
polyfit needs a constant column
quiz.explain: np.polyfit(x, y, 1); Excel's SLOPE takes y first. Swapped arguments give a different line (→ section 1, 'Fitting it').

quiz.q: The residual plot of payment ~ principal shows three bands, one per term. What does it mean?
options: The line is perfect
The model is missing the term: add it as a predictor (or fit each term separately)
Delete the 24-month loans
R² must be 1
quiz.explain: Residuals that differ by group point to the missing variable (→ section 1, 'Residuals', worked example Step 6).

quiz.q: Which loan pulls the Auto line most if its payment is mistyped?
options: One at the average principal
One with the largest principal — the highest leverage
Any loan equally
The one with the smallest payment
quiz.explain: Leverage grows with (x − x̄)²; an error far from the average x tilts the line most (→ section 1, 'Outliers and leverage').

quiz.q: The Micro line (fitted on 0.5–5 m loans) says a 300 m loan pays 81.5 m a month. What is the problem?
options: None — R² is 0.665
Extrapolation: 300 m is far outside the range the line was fitted on
The slope is negative
The intercept is too large
quiz.explain: A line is a rule only inside the data's range; real 300 m SME loans pay about 16 m (→ section 1, 'Extrapolation').

quiz.q: Company corner: why is PTI on the owner's personal income meaningless for SME loans?
options: SME loans have no payment
The business repays them from its cash flow, so personal income is the wrong denominator (median PTI 151 %)
SME incomes are not recorded
PTI only works for 0 % loans
quiz.explain: A ratio needs the right denominator; for a business loan it is the business's cash flow (→ Company corner).

w09d2.t: Week 9 · Day 2 — Logistic regression and the scorecard: from a score to a probability of going bad

quiz.q: The probability of bad is 10 %. What are the odds of bad? (3 decimals)
quiz.explain: 0.1 / 0.9 = 0.111: one bad per nine good (→ section 1, 'Probability, odds and log-odds').

quiz.q: Why not fit a straight line to bad (0/1) against the score?
options: It is too slow
It predicts impossible probabilities — below 0 above a score of 760 — and assumes the same change per point everywhere
It cannot use scores
It always gives R² = 0
quiz.explain: The linear probability model runs out of [0, 1]: −3.3 % at 850 (→ section 1, 'Why a straight line fails').

quiz.q: In logistic regression, what is a straight line in the score?
options: The probability
The log-odds of bad
The odds
The bad count
quiz.explain: z = β₀ + β₁ · score is the log-odds; the sigmoid turns it into a probability (→ section 1, 'The logistic curve').

quiz.q: What does maximum likelihood make as small as possible?
options: The squared residuals
The log-loss
The number of wrong calls at 50 %
The PDO
quiz.explain: Highest likelihood = lowest log-loss: −ln p for bad loans, −ln(1 − p) for good ones (→ section 1, 'Fitting it').

quiz.q: e^(100 · β₁) = 0.275 for our score. What does it mean?
options: 100 more points lower the PD by 27.5 points
100 more points multiply the odds of going bad by 0.275 — about a quarter
27.5 % of loans go bad
The PDO is 27.5
quiz.explain: An odds ratio multiplies odds; the odds halve every ln 2 / 0.012903 = 53.7 points (→ section 1, 'A coefficient as an odds ratio').

quiz.q: A card has 600 points at good:bad odds of 50:1 and PDO 20. What odds does 640 have, good per bad?
quiz.explain: Two PDOs, two doublings: 50 × 4 = 200 (→ section 1, 'The scorecard').

quiz.q: Which statement about Nur's grades is right?
options: They are separate from the score
They are score bands: A 720+, B 660–719, C 600–659, D below 600, with bad rates 0.93 / 1.88 / 5.12 / 10.91 %
D is the safest grade
Grades have no bad rate
quiz.explain: Every grade boundary is a cut-off on the score (→ section 1, 'Risk grades A–D').

quiz.q: A vendor's model is '97 % accurate' on our loans. Why is that no news?
options: Saying 'good' to everyone is 97.07 % accurate when 2.93 % go bad
97 % is low
Accuracy is always 97 %
Vendors cannot measure accuracy
quiz.explain: With a rare outcome, judge ranking, calibration and log-loss, not accuracy (→ section 1, '3 % bads').

quiz.q: Company corner: what is an out-of-time sample for?
options: Fitting the model faster
Testing the model on a later period it never saw, as it will be used
Removing old loans
Choosing the PDO
quiz.explain: A scorecard is used on future applicants; validation on a later period is the honest test (→ Company corner).

w09d3.t: Week 9 · Day 3 — Is the scorecard any good? ROC, AUC, Gini, KS and lift

quiz.q: Only 2.93 % of Nur's scored loans are bad. Why is accuracy a poor way to judge the scorecard?
options: Approving everyone is already 97.07 % accurate, while catching no bad at all
Accuracy cannot be computed for scores
Accuracy is always below 50 %
Accuracy needs a perfect scorecard
quiz.explain: The big class dominates: 'every loan is good' is right 7 392 times in 7 615. Use TPR and FPR at a cut-off, AUC or Gini for the ranking (→ section 1, 'Accuracy').

quiz.q: At a cut-off, the score declines 37 bads (of 223) and 294 goods (of 7 392). Which point is that on the ROC curve?
quiz.explain: The ROC curve plots (FPR, TPR): FPR = 294 / 7 392 = 4.0 %, TPR = 37 / 223 = 16.6 % (→ section 1, 'The ROC curve').

quiz.q: What does an AUC of 0.5 mean?
options: Half the loans are approved
The score ranks no better than a coin toss — its ROC curve is the diagonal
Half the bads are caught
The Gini is 0.5
quiz.explain: A random good outscores a random bad half the time; Gini = 2 × 0.5 − 1 = 0 (→ section 1, 'AUC', 'Gini').

quiz.q: Our score's AUC is 0.689. What is its Gini, to 3 decimals?
quiz.explain: 2 × 0.689 − 1 = 0.377 — below the 0.4–0.6 usual for an application scorecard (→ section 1, 'Gini').

quiz.q: What does this print for our loans (a high score means a good loan)?
quiz.code:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
roc_auc_score(y, s)
options: 0.311 — the AUC of the score read backwards
An error
quiz.explain: roc_auc_score expects a higher value for the positive class (bad). Pass -s to get 0.689 (→ section 1, 'AUC').

quiz.q: KS is the…
options: Area under the ROC curve
Widest gap between the cumulative shares of bads and goods, max(TPR − FPR)
Bad rate of the worst decile
Share of correct decisions
quiz.explain: Ours: 0.34 at 658, where 65.9 % of bads and 32.0 % of goods score at or below (→ section 1, 'KS').

quiz.q: The worst 10 % of scores hold 25.1 % of the bads. What is their lift, to 2 decimals?
quiz.explain: Gain ÷ share of loans = 25.1 / 10 = 2.51: their bad rate is two and a half times the average (→ section 1, 'Lift and gains').

quiz.q: 2024 loans: Gini 0.415 (95 % interval 0.28–0.54). 2025–26 loans: 0.365 (0.28–0.45). What is the fair reading?
options: The score has failed and must be replaced
Lower on the new loans, but well within noise: keep monitoring
The new loans are safer
The intervals prove there is no change at all
quiz.explain: Overlapping intervals are no proof of a fall — and no proof of 'no change' either: the honest word is 'watch' (→ section 1, 'Out-of-time validation').

quiz.q: Company corner: a validator's three questions, in order, are…
options: Accuracy, precision, recall
Does it rank, does it predict the right level, is it stable
Gini, Gini by product, Gini by year
Who built it, when, with what tool
quiz.explain: Discrimination (Gini, KS), calibration (predicted vs actual by band), stability (PSI) (→ Company corner).

w09d4.t: Week 9 · Day 4 — The cut-off and watching the model: approval, bad rate, profit, PSI

quiz.q: Raising the cut-off from 600 to 660 moves the approval rate from 95.7 % to 66.7 % and the bad rate from 2.55 % to 1.50 %. What does that show?
options: The trade-off: a large loss of volume for a small fall in bad rate
That 660 is the best line
That the score is broken
That the bad rate rises with the cut-off
quiz.explain: 29 points of approvals for about one point of bad rate — whether it is worth it is a question of money (→ section 1, 'The cut-off').

quiz.q: A good loan leaves 1 454 907 soum, a bad one costs 17 219 143. What is the break-even bad rate, in %, to 2 decimals?
quiz.explain: 1 454 907 ÷ 18 674 050 = 7.79 % — W8D2's break-even PD for a Consumer loan (→ section 1, 'The profit-maximising cut-off').

quiz.q: Funding rises from 18 % to 22 %. What happens to the profit-maximising cut-off?
options: It moves up (594 → 659): a good loan leaves less, so fewer groups are worth lending to
It moves down
It stays: the cut-off depends only on the score
There is no longer a best cut-off
quiz.explain: The break-even falls to 3.72 %, below grade C's 5 %: the line jumps to the C/B edge (→ section 1, explorer).

quiz.q: The committee wants approved loans under 2 % bad. The loosest such line is 647, earning 6.12 bn; the best line earns 7.14 bn. What do you tell them?
options: The target costs about 1.0 bn of profit on this book — vote with that number in view
647 is the best line
The target is free
Targets are not allowed
quiz.explain: The price of a target is a fact the committee needs before it votes (→ section 1, 'A bad-rate target').

quiz.q: Which applicants are swap-ins?
options: Approved today and declined by the new rule
Rejected today and approved by the new rule — their outcomes are unknown
Applicants with no score
Loans that were written off
quiz.explain: Swap-outs are known (Nur lent to them); swap-ins are not — reject inference (→ section 1, 'Swap-in and swap-out').

quiz.q: What does this print?
quiz.code:
e = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
a = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e))
options: 0.0 — identical shares, no shift
An error
quiz.explain: Each band's term is (a − e) × ln(a / e) = 0 × ln 1 = 0 (→ section 1, 'PSI').

quiz.q: The PSI is 0.18. What is the reading, and the next step?
options: Stable; nothing to do
Watch: find which input moved with the CSIs and check the bad rate by band there
Act: switch the scorecard off today
PSI above 0.1 means the Gini has fallen
quiz.explain: 0.1–0.25 is amber: investigate the cause before acting. PSI says the population moved, not that the ranking broke (→ section 1, 'CSI', 'What to do').

quiz.q: The bad rate of new vintages rises from 2.9 % to 4.1 % while the Gini and the PSI stay the same. What is the usual action?
options: Rebuild the scorecard
Recalibrate the PD levels and move the cut-off: the order is right, the level is not
Ignore it
Lower the cut-off
quiz.explain: Ranking intact, level shifted: recalibrate and reprice rather than rebuild (→ section 1, 'What to do when it drifts').

quiz.q: Company corner: where does an approved cut-off live?
options: In the analyst's notebook
In the credit policy, changed only by the risk committee
In the bureau's database
In each officer's head
quiz.explain: The policy holds the cut-offs, rules, limits, overrides and monitoring triggers; the committee changes it (→ Company corner).

w09d5.t: Week 9 · Day 5 — Checkpoint: the scorecard review for the risk committee

quiz.q: A scorecard's AUC is 0.72. What is its Gini (2 decimals)?
quiz.explain: Gini = 2 × AUC − 1 = 2 × 0.72 − 1 = 0.44; a coin has AUC 0.5 and Gini 0 (→ A1).

quiz.q: Our score: a higher score means a safer loan. This prints 0.311. What went wrong?
quiz.code:
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
roc_auc_score(sc["bad"], sc["credit_score"])
options: Nothing — the score ranks worse than a coin
roc_auc_score needs probabilities, not scores
The direction: it asks how well a HIGH score finds a BAD loan; with 1 − bad (or −score) it becomes 1 − 0.311
The loans without a score
quiz.explain: The same score read the other way round gives one minus the AUC; check the direction before you report (→ A1, mistakes).

quiz.q: A scorecard has KS = 0.30 at score 650. What does that say?
options: 30 % of the loans score below 650
At 650 the share of bads scoring at or below it exceeds the share of goods by 30 points — the widest gap anywhere
650 is the cut-off that earns most
30 % of the bads are refused at 650
quiz.explain: KS is the widest gap between two cumulative curves; the cut-off that earns most is a different question, answered with money (→ A1, C2).

quiz.q: The 2026 loans give a lower Gini than the older loans — on a few dozen bads, all from loans of the first months of the year. What do you tell the committee?
options: The scorecard broke in 2026 — rebuild it
2026 borrowers are safer, so the Gini fell
No evidence of decay yet: few bads on young loans and a wide interval — read it again when they reach 12 months on book
Out-of-time checks cannot be done on a live portfolio
quiz.explain: Out of time, compare loans of the same age, and give every Gini its bads and its interval (→ A3).

quiz.q: This month's applicants against the development sample: PSI = 0.18. What do you do?
options: Nothing — it is under 0.25
Watch: find which characteristic moved (CSI) and why, check the Gini on recent mature loans, keep the cut-off under review
Rebuild the scorecard today
Lower the cut-off to approve more
quiz.explain: 0.1–0.25 is 'watch': a shift to explain, not yet a broken model (→ B1).

quiz.q: Why does the committee's stability line use the applicants' scores, not the approved loans'?
options: Loans have no scores
Applicants are what the scorecard sees; the loans have passed the decision, so their shift mixes the population with the approval policy
The applicants' PSI is always smaller
Applicants are more numerous, so their PSI is exact
quiz.explain: Between the applicant and the loan sits the decision; a change in it moves the loans' PSI with no change in who applies (→ B2).

quiz.q: A product's break-even PD is 6 %. One score band goes bad 8 % of the time; the band above it, 4 %. Where does the profit-maximising cut-off go?
options: Below both bands — approve everyone
Between them: refuse the 8 % band, keep the 4 % band
Above both bands — the lower the bad rate, the better
It cannot be told without the Gini
quiz.explain: Drop a band while it loses money (its bad rate above the break-even); above that, nearly every refused loan would have paid (→ C2, C3).

quiz.q: Which belong in the memo's cut-off recommendation?
options: The cut-off, with its approval share and bad rate
The profit change, with the assumptions under it
Who is refused (the swap-out set) and what that costs
The full Python code
How it is rolled out and when it is read again
The cut-off with the lowest bad rate, whatever it costs
quiz.explain: A decision, its money, its cost in customers and its rollout; the code stays in the notebook (→ Part D).

quiz.q: The policy that keeps running for most applicants while a new one is tried on a random share is called the … (one word).
quiz.explain: Champion / challenger: the challenger runs on a random share, and both are read on loans of the same age (→ C3, Day 4).

w09d6.t: Week 9 · Day 6 — Final exam: credit risk and the whole course

quiz.q: Across all customers, income and the requested amount have r = 0.002. A colleague writes "no relationship". What is the careful wording?
options: Correct: r near 0 means the variables are independent
r measures only straight-line links. Say "no straight-line link" and look at the scatter plot or at Spearman
r near 0 means the data are wrong
The two columns must be swapped
quiz.explain: A curve can have r = 0 and still be a strong link. r says how close the dots are to a straight line (→ Week 9 · Day 1, r = 0 — no straight line, not no link).

quiz.q: A fitted line has a correlation of r = −0.8. What is R², in %?
quiz.explain: R² = r² = 0.64, so the line explains 64 % of the spread of the payment. Squaring removes the minus sign (→ Week 9 · Day 1, R²).

quiz.q: The Auto line is a = −12.1 and b = 41.49 (payment in thousand soum, principal in m soum), fitted on 50–400 m loans. What monthly payment does it give for a 250 m Auto loan, in thousand soum (nearest whole number)?
quiz.explain: −12.1 + 41.49 × 250 = 10 360 thousand soum, about 10.4 m soum a month. 250 m is inside the 50–400 m range the line was fitted on (→ Week 9 · Day 1, The least-squares line).

quiz.q: A line for the payment against the principal was fitted on Micro loans of 0.5 to 5 m soum. Someone uses it to quote a 40 m loan. What do you say?
options: Fine, the R² is high
Do not: 40 m is far outside the range the line was fitted on, so the answer is a guess, not a rule
Fine, if you add the intercept
Fine, if you take the log
quiz.explain: A line is a rule only inside the data's range. Say the range next to every rule (→ Week 9 · Day 1, Prediction against explanation, and the extrapolation trap).

quiz.q: A grade has odds of bad of 1 to 19 (one bad for every 19 good). What is the probability of bad, in %?
quiz.explain: p = odds / (1 + odds) = (1/19) / (20/19) = 1/20 = 5 % (→ Week 9 · Day 2, Probability, odds and log-odds).

quiz.q: In the score model e^(50 · β₁) = 0.525. A customer's score is 50 points higher. What happens?
options: The probability of going bad falls by 47.5 percentage points
The odds of going bad are multiplied by 0.525, so they are about halved
The probability of going bad is multiplied by 0.525
The score is 52.5 % better
quiz.explain: An odds ratio multiplies odds, not probabilities. For small probabilities the two are close, but they are not the same thing (→ Week 9 · Day 2, A coefficient as an odds ratio).

quiz.q: A scorecard gives 600 points at good:bad odds of 40:1 and has PDO 30. What good:bad odds does a score of 570 have? Give the first number of x:1.
quiz.explain: PDO is the number of points that doubles the odds. 570 is one PDO below 600, so the odds halve: 40 → 20 (→ Week 9 · Day 2, The scorecard — points, base score and PDO).

quiz.q: On the development data the model's predicted bads add up to exactly the actual number of bads. Does that prove it is well calibrated?
options: Yes: total predicted = total actual
No: on the total this holds by construction. Check predicted against actual by score band, and on later loans
Yes, if the Gini is above 0.4
No: calibration is not defined for logistic regression
quiz.explain: A model can rank well and still be badly calibrated. The check that counts is band by band and out of time (→ Week 9 · Day 2, Calibration — predicted against actual; Mistakes people make).

quiz.q: Which statements about AUC and Gini are true?
options: AUC is the chance that a random good loan scores above a random bad loan, ties counted half
Gini = 2 × AUC − 1, so a Gini of 0.50 is an AUC of 0.75
An AUC of 0.5 means the score ranks no better than a coin toss
A Gini of 0.38 means the score is right for 38 % of the loans
AUC depends on the cut-off you choose
quiz.explain: AUC and Gini measure ranking across every cut-off, not accuracy at one of them. Always give a Gini with its number of bads (→ Week 9 · Day 3, AUC; Gini).

quiz.q: The scored loans hold 240 bads and 6 000 goods. At one cut-off the score refuses 60 bads and 420 goods. What is the false-positive rate, in %?
quiz.explain: FPR = goods refused ÷ all goods = 420 / 6 000 = 7 %. TPR = bads refused ÷ all bads = 60 / 240 = 25 %. The ROC curve plots (FPR, TPR) for every cut-off (→ Week 9 · Day 3, TPR and FPR; The ROC curve).

quiz.q: The worst-scored 5 % of the loans hold 15 % of all the bads. What is their lift (one decimal)?
quiz.explain: Lift = share of the bads ÷ share of the loans = 15 / 5 = 3.0: their bad rate is three times the average (→ Week 9 · Day 3, Lift and gains).

quiz.q: The Gini of last quarter's loans is lower than the Gini of older loans. Why can this be misleading?
options: Last quarter's loans are young: few have had time to go bad, so the Gini rests on few bads and is noisy. Compare loans of the same age and give an interval
Young loans always have a higher Gini
The Gini cannot be computed on recent loans
Older loans are always better
quiz.explain: Maturity is the trap of out-of-time checks. Give every Gini its number of bads and its interval (→ Week 9 · Day 3, Out-of-time validation).

quiz.q: A good loan leaves 900 000 soum. A bad loan costs 12 000 000 soum. A score band is worth lending to only while its bad rate stays below the break-even. What is the break-even bad rate, in % (two decimals)?
quiz.explain: Break-even = good ÷ (good + bad) = 900 000 / 12 900 000 = 6.98 %. A band below it pays; a band above it loses money (→ Week 9 · Day 4, The profit-maximising cut-off and the break-even bad rate).

quiz.q: You want to test a stricter cut-off. Which design is right?
options: Switch everyone to the new cut-off and compare with last year

Run the new cut-off (the challenger) on a random share of new applications at the same time as the current one (the champion), with the size and length fixed in advance. Read both on loans of the same age
Run the new cut-off in one branch only
Test it on last year's rejected applicants
quiz.explain: A random share at the same time means season, marketing and the economy hit both arms alike. The champion also keeps showing what the refused would have done (→ Week 9 · Day 4, Champion / challenger).

quiz.q: What does this return (three decimals)? A PSI below 0.1 reads as stable.
quiz.code:
e = np.array([0.5, 0.5])   # development sample: shares of two score bands
a = np.array([0.6, 0.4])   # this month's applicants
np.sum((a - e) * np.log(a / e))

quiz.q: Four loans, ordered by principal from the largest: 90, 80, 80, 70. What do RANK() and DENSE_RANK() give the loan with 70?
options: 3 and 3
4 and 3
4 and 4
3 and 4
quiz.explain: RANK skips after a tie (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK does not (1, 2, 2, 3). ROW_NUMBER never repeats (→ Week 3 · Day 2, RANK and DENSE_RANK).

quiz.q: closed_at is empty for the loans that are still open. What does this return?
quiz.code:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans
WHERE disbursed_at NOT IN (SELECT closed_at FROM loans);
quiz.explain: One NULL in the subquery's list makes NOT IN unknown for every row, so no row passes. Add WHERE closed_at IS NOT NULL inside, or use NOT EXISTS (→ Week 3 · Day 3, IN with a subquery).

quiz.q: customers_clean must keep the original, earliest row of each duplicated customer. Remove Duplicates keeps the first row it meets. What do you do before it?
options: Sort by registered_at, oldest first
Nothing: Excel keeps the oldest on its own
Sort by customer_id, largest first
Tick every column
quiz.explain: Remove Duplicates keeps the first row it meets, so the order decides which copy survives (→ Week 4 · Day 5, customers_clean).

quiz.q: You expected len(m) == 92 193, one row per instalment. It is smaller. Why?
quiz.code:
m = inst.merge(paid, on="installment_id")
len(inst), len(m)
options: merge defaults to how="inner", so instalments with no payment vanish. Use how="left" and check the length
merge sorts and drops ties
pandas rounds the keys
installment_id must be a string
quiz.explain: The default join is inner. The instalments with no payment are exactly the ones DPD needs. Add validate= and an assert on the length (→ Week 5 · Day 3, merge).

quiz.q: A test shows that the app channel is riskier when it is not, and the channel is cut. Which error is this, and what controls its probability?
options: Type I, controlled by α
Type II, controlled by α
Type I, controlled by the power
Type II, controlled by n only
quiz.explain: Rejecting a true H₀ is a type I error. Its probability is α, which you fix before the data. A type II error, missing a real effect, has probability β, and power is 1 − β (→ Week 6 · Day 3, α, type I and type II errors, power).

quiz.q: App FPD is 1.70 % and branch FPD is 1.04 %. What is the relative risk of an FPD in the app against the branches (two decimals)?
quiz.explain: RR = 1.70 / 1.04 = 1.63 (from the exact rates 41 / 2 411 and 34 / 3 263). It is a ratio of two rates and needs its interval: 1.04 to 2.56. The difference in points and in FPDs per 1 000 loans is the companion number (→ Week 6 · Day 3, Effect size).

quiz.q: A user's variant is decided by hashing the user id together with a text that is different in every experiment, usually the experiment's name. What is that text called? (one word)
quiz.explain: The salt makes assignments independent across experiments. With the same salt the same users would land in B every time, and two tests would be perfectly correlated (→ Week 7 · Day 1, Randomisation and assignment).

quiz.q: On a card, what happens when [Due] is 0 or blank, and what should you write instead?
quiz.code: Collection Rate = [Paid] / [Due]
options: It shows the company total
It shows an error or infinity instead of a blank. Write DIVIDE ( [Paid], [Due] )
Power BI hides the card
It shows 0 %, which is fine
quiz.explain: DIVIDE returns blank, or a value you choose, when the denominator is 0 or blank. Use it for every ratio (→ Week 7 · Day 4, The first measures).

quiz.q: Loan 8 is a 6-month Micro loan of 3 360 000 soum. At 18 % a year (1.5 % a month), the funding costs 181 445 soum on the falling balance. What would it cost if it were charged on the full principal for all six months?
quiz.explain: 3 360 000 × 1.5 % × 6 = 302 400, about two thirds too much. Funding runs on the balance owed, which falls with every instalment (→ Week 8 · Day 2, Cost of funds).

quiz.q: Interviewer: "FPD in the app doubled last month." The month had about 120 app loans, and defaults went from 1 to 2. What is your first step?
options: Pause the app
Check that it is real and how big: "doubled" is one more default on about 120 loans, which is noise until the interval and the definition say otherwise
Look for a fraud ring
Re-train the scorecard
quiz.explain: Most candidates skip "is it real and how big". Only then do you locate it, separate mix from rate and recommend (→ Week 8 · Day 5, B3).
